sens: Live together, share daily life with someone
Live in communion with Christ, both now and for eternity
G4800.detail:
1. The most direct meaning is to live together, sharing one's daily existence with someone else. When Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 7:3 that he carries the Corinthians "to life and death," he evokes the intimacy of those who live side by side, inseparable in joys as well as in sorrows.
2. However, the word takes on a profound spiritual dimension in Paul’s writings: to live with Christ means to be united to Him, to live in intimate communion with Him, both in this present life and in the eternity to come. In Romans 6:8 and 2 Timothy 2:11, this paradoxical expression — "if we have died with Him, we will also live with Him" — reveals that the believer's death with Christ (through baptism) is the path that unites him to His resurrected life. It is a new life, a new existence shared with the risen Christ.
G4800.origine: The word is composed of the prefix συν (sun, "with") and the verb ζάω (zaō, "to live"). This combination emphasizes the idea of a shared life with someone else. It is a typically Greek construction to express union or communion. The basic image is very simple: two people living together, but Paul elevates it to a mystical level by applying it to the union of the believer with the risen Christ.
G4800.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the New Testament, and only in Paul’s writings. In Romans 6:8 and 2 Timothy 2:11, it describes the future life of the believer with the risen Christ, as the culmination of dying with Him in baptism — this is the heart of Pauline theology of union with Christ. In 2 Corinthians 7:3, in a more emotional context, the derived noun (“life”) speaks of the intimacy between Paul and the Corinthians. Its use is rare and solemn, marking each time a major spiritual reality: the union of the believer with the living Christ.
G4800.portee: This word reminds the Christian that their faith is not an abstract doctrine, but a life shared with Christ. To be saved is to pass from spiritual death to a new life in communion with the risen Christ — a life that begins now and continues into eternity. It is a call to recognize the intimacy of this union and to live it out concretely, every day.

sens: Yoke together two animals under the same yoke
Unite together two things or two beings to make them one
G4801.detail:
1. The base word evokes the image of a yoke: it is to join two draft animals (like two oxen) so that they pull together. It is a word from rural life that every reader of Jesus would understand.
2. By extension, the verb takes on a figurative meaning: it signifies to unite in general, to bind together. It is in this sense that Jesus uses it to speak of marriage: when a man and a woman become husband and wife, God joins them (Matthew 19:6). They are no longer two separate beings, but "one flesh." Marriage is this complete union that God performs.
G4801.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb zeugnyō (zeug-), which means "to yoke" or "to join under the yoke." The prefix syn- (together) reinforces the idea: sy-zeugnyō = to join together. The word zeugos refers to the yoke itself, the wood that connects two animals. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb translates the Hebrew hâbar, which means "to join" or "to bind together." The image of the yoke — which unites without destroying each animal — aptly conveys the biblical idea of marriage: two beings remain distinct but are united for the same path.
G4801.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, and always in Matthew and Mark, in the same passage: Jesus responding to the Pharisees about divorce. When asked if it is permissible to divorce his wife, Jesus responds by going back to Genesis: "God joined them" (Matthew 19:6, Mark 10:9). Marriage is not a temporary contract that man can break; it is a union that God performs. Jesus uses this word to show that marriage comes from God and that man should not dissolve it. The use of the past tense (“joined”) indicates that God acts at the moment of marriage, and it is this divine act that creates the indissoluble bond.
G4801.portee: This word reminds us that Christian marriage is not a human arrangement, but a covenant that God Himself seals. In hearing this, the believer understands that marriage has a sacred gravity and dignity: what God has joined, man must not separate (Matthew 19:6). It is a call to honor marriage as a work of God, not as a revocable contract to be taken lightly.

sens: exchange words on a subject, seeking together to understand or explore it
debate face to face, expressing opposing positions or questioning
ask each other, pose a question together without arriving at a certain answer
G4802.detail:
1. To discuss means to examine a subject together through words. In Mark 12:28, a scribe who has heard Jesus and the Sadducees discussing approaches to continue the exchange: it is a conversation where each listens and contributes. It is to seek understanding through speaking.

2. To discuss can also mean to debate, to confront one’s ideas with others, sometimes even to contest them. In Mark 8:11, the Pharisees "discuss" with Jesus seeking to test Him with questions — this is not a simple chat, but a courteous confrontation. Similarly, in Mark 9:14, the scribes discuss with the disciples: there is tension, a divergence.

3. To mutually ask is to share a perplexity, a question. In Mark 1:27, after witnessing a miracle, the people "ask" one another: "What is this?" No one has the answer, everyone is questioning together. Likewise, in Mark 9:10: upon hearing Jesus speak of resurrection, the disciples wonder among themselves what this means.
G4802.origine: The word comes from the Greek root ζητέω (zêteō = to seek, to search) preceded by the prefix συν (syn = with, together). Literally: to seek together. This formation expresses the idea that one is not seeking alone, but in interaction. The basic image is that of a common search, sharing an inquiry or reflection.
G4802.emploi: The verb appears 10 times in the New Testament, mostly in Mark (6 times) and in Acts (2 times). It usually describes moments when people exchange thoughts on an important subject. With the disciples and the crowd, Jesus and His opponents "discuss" the meaning of His actions or the significance of His words (Mark 1:27, 9:10, 12:28, Luke 24:15). The Pharisees "discuss" with Jesus to test or confront Him (Mark 8:11). The apostles "discuss" with their opponents in Jerusalem or in the diaspora (Acts 6:9, 9:29). The word always emphasizes an active exchange, never a simple unilateral announcement.
G4802.portee: This word shows us that the New Testament values discussion as a means of seeking truth and progressing in faith. It is an invitation for Christians not to fear questions or debates, but to experience them as a form of communion in the search. Even in the face of opposition or perplexity, discussing together — rather than remaining alone in misunderstanding — is a biblical way to advance.

sens: debate between several people
dispute, quarrel
joint search for truth
G4803.detail: 1. A discussion is an exchange of words between several people expressing their opinions. This is the most natural meaning of the word: people talking together to debate an issue. 2. The word can also refer to a quarrel, a somewhat heated dispute between interlocutors who do not agree — less a fight than a confrontation of opinions. In Acts 28:29, the Jews in Rome have a discussion with Paul, meaning a contradictory debate where positions oppose each other. 3. In a more noble sense, it is also a common search: when we truly discuss, we seek to understand the truth together, exchanging arguments and questions.
G4803.origine: The word comes from the prefix "with" (syn) and a root meaning "to seek" or "to examine" (zêtê). Etymologically, it means "to seek together." The Greek family also includes the verb suzêteô (to discuss) and the noun zêtêsis (search, question). The word primarily evokes the image of an inquiry conducted by multiple voices.
G4803.emploi: The word appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 28:29. Paul, a prisoner in Rome, receives the Jews of the city and preaches to them about the kingdom of God. After his speech, they begin to discuss among themselves — a lively discussion since they do not agree and leave. This context shows that the discussion here is less cordial than a true religious dispute about Jesus and salvation.
G4803.portee: The word reminds us that the Christian faith is not afraid of dialogue: Paul does not shy away from discussion, he confronts it. But it also shows that discussion alone does not convert: it can leave hearts closed. For the believer, it is an invitation to seek the truth together in respect, while knowing that only the Spirit of God can change a life.

sens: One who loves to discuss, who engages in controversy
A person who contests or questions
One who practices dialectics, the art of argumentation
G4804.detail:
1. A disputant is someone who has the habit and pleasure of discussing, debating extensively on all subjects. It is a person who loves to argue, who does not let anything pass without questioning or examining it through dialogue. In 1 Corinthians 1:20, Paul refers to the one who represents the human wisdom of his time, always busy contesting and arguing.
2. By extension, it is one who actively contests, who opposes through words and reasoning. The term emphasizes the action of disputing, that is, supporting a position through discussion and verbal exchange, often persistently.
3. In a Greek context, the disputant recalls the sophists and philosophers who excelled in the art of debate and logical argumentation. It is a person trained in these techniques of public discussion.
G4804.origine: The word comes from the verb συνζητέω (suzétéô), which means "to discuss together, to dispute." It is composed of συν (sun, "with") and ζητέω (zétéô, "to seek, to examine"). The basic idea is that of seeking together through words and debate. The suffix -τής adds the idea of a person who makes a profession or habit of this activity. That is why the disputant is one who habitually discusses and argues.
G4804.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 1:20. Paul uses it to criticize the wisdom of the world and its representatives: the wise, the scribes, and specifically the "disputants," those who believe they can solve all problems through discussion and argumentation. In this context, Paul shows that this human wisdom, based on debate and dialectics, has become folly in the eyes of God. The term thus carries a slightly critical connotation: the one who disputes clings to human reason and ignores divine revelation.
G4804.portee: This word invites the Christian to reflect on the danger of becoming trapped in dispute and argumentation without seeking the truth beyond the mere forces of reason. Paul reminds us that the wisdom of God, revealed in the crucified Christ, surpasses and judges the wisdom of the world. For the believer, this means not making perpetual discussion an end in itself, but seeking to hear and follow the word of God, which alone saves.

sens: person who shares the same yoke, the same work
co-worker
one who helps in the same cause
G4805.detail:
1. The word evokes the image of a yoke: two animals bound under the same yoke work together. Paul uses it figuratively to refer to one who helps him in his ministry — someone engaged alongside him in the same apostolic task (Philippians 4:3).
2. It is a co-worker, but a faithful, proven companion, trustworthy. Paul addresses this letter to a "faithful colleague": the word is an expression of affection and esteem for one who shares the burden.
3. Beyond mere work, it is a communion in the same cause: the Gospel. The colleague is not just a simple assistant, but someone who has committed to fight alongside Paul for the faith.
G4805.origine: The Greek word σύζυγος comes from σύν ("with") and ζυγός ("yoke"). The image is agricultural: a yoke binds two draft animals to make them work together. The Greeks used it literally to refer to one animal harnessed to another, and then figuratively for a companion, an associate. It is a rare word in the New Testament, created or renewed by Paul to express an intimacy of apostolic work.
G4805.emploi: The word appears only once in the Segond in Philippians 4:3. Paul asks this "faithful colleague" to help two women, Euodia and Syntyche, who "have contended for the Gospel" with him. These women are themselves described as his colleagues: they have led the pastoral fight alongside him. The term reveals that Paul did not exercise his ministry alone, but in a team, sharing the burden with other workers dedicated to the same mission.
G4805.portee: For the Christian today, this word emphasizes that the life of faith is not solitary: God gives us companions in work. Being "under the same yoke" means sharing not only tasks but a common vision and commitment to the Gospel. It is a call to recognize those who toil with us and to engage solidly alongside them.

sens: Give life together, resurrect with someone
Restore spiritual life through divine forgiveness
G4806.detail:
1. The Greek word combines three elements: "together" (syn-), "life" (zôo-), and "produce/make" (-poieô). It expresses the action of making alive together, particularly in the sense of resurrecting with someone. In Colossians 2:13, God "made you alive together with him": He restores spiritual life to people who were dead in sin, and He does this by uniting them with Christ in this new existence.
2. Metaphorically, this verb denotes the restoration of spiritual life. In Ephesians 2:5, Paul says that God "made us alive together with Christ": the believer, once spiritually dead in sin, comes to life by the grace of God, not alone, but incorporated into Christ. It is a shared rebirth with Him.
G4806.origine: The verb is formed from the prefix syn- ("with," "together") combined with zôopoieô ("to make alive, resurrect"), which itself comes from zôé ("life") and poieô ("to make, produce"). This composition emphasizes the idea of a shared, simultaneous vital action. The word literally expresses the action of "co-vivifying" or "making alive together." It is rare in the New Testament and appears only in Paul.
G4806.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Paul. In Ephesians 2:5, it describes how God made alive together — with Christ — those who were spiritually dead in sin. In Colossians 2:13, it reappears in a very similar context: God made alive those who were "dead in your trespasses" by grafting them into the life of Christ and granting them forgiveness. In both cases, the verb emphasizes the believer's union with Christ in resurrection and new life, through divine grace.
G4806.portee: This word reveals a profound truth for the Christian: the new life is not an isolated or personal matter, but a life lived "with Christ." It does not depend on personal effort, but on God's forgiveness and grace. When Paul speaks of making us alive "together" with Christ, he invites the believer to see themselves as participating in the resurrection of Jesus himself, not by their merits, but by the love and mercy of God.

sens: Fruit tree producing edible berries
Symbol of what is difficult to uproot or move
G4807.detail:
1. The mulberry is a fruit tree that bears black or red berries (called mulberries) that are highly valued. It is a sturdy tree with deep roots. In Luke 17:6, Jesus uses the mulberry as an example of something that could only be moved by the power of exceptional faith: "If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mulberry: 'Be uprooted and planted in the sea'; and it would obey you."
2. Figuratively, the mulberry represents what seems impossible to change or uproot by our own strength. Its choice by Jesus underscores the solidity and depth of its roots, making its uprooting miraculously improbable.
G4807.origine: The Greek word sukaminos specifically refers to the mulberry (tree of the genus Morus), distinct from the sycamore (Greek term: sukomorea), although the two names can be confusing in some older translations. In biblical Hebrew, the corresponding term is shiqmah, which also refers to the wild fig or Egyptian sycamore. The Greek word likely comes from a Semitic root, attesting to the commercial and botanical contacts between the Greek world and the Middle East.
G4807.emploi: The mulberry appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 17:6. Jesus uses it to illustrate the power of faith: he imagines a disciple commanding the mulberry to be uprooted and planted in the sea, and it happening immediately. This choice of the mulberry is not insignificant: it is a tree with very deep and difficult-to-upright roots, making it a powerful symbol of what is firmly established and seems impossible to move. Jesus asserts that authentic faith, even tiny ("like a grain of mustard seed"), can accomplish the humanly impossible.
G4807.portee: This passage teaches the Christian that true faith is not a matter of quantity but of quality and trust in God. The mulberry symbolizes the obstacles we deem insurmountable: illness, circumstances, our fears. Jesus promises that those who possess true faith in God will see extraordinary things accomplished. It is a call not to reduce faith to an external matter of size, but to recognize its transforming power, even when it seems minuscule.

sens: Fruit tree with broad leaves that produces figs
Image of nature and its cycles
Sign of imminence or divine judgment
Symbol of barrenness or unfruitfulness
G4808.detail:
1. The fig tree is a common fruit tree in the Mediterranean, with broad leaves and sweet fruits. It is one of the most present trees in biblical daily life, alongside the olive tree and the palm tree. It is cultivated in vineyards (Luke 13:6), and its leaves appear before its fruits.

2. Jesus uses it to teach the laws of nature: "Look at the fig tree and all the trees" (Luke 21:29) — it is a familiar example of the regular progression of seasons, which prepares to recognize the signs announcing the return of Christ.

3. This tree becomes a sign of judgment in the episode where Jesus curses it (Matthew 21:19-21, Mark 11:13-21): it bears no fruit while it has leaves, signaling a deceptive promise. Its instant withering symbolizes judgment on unfruitfulness and hypocrisy.

4. The fig tree also represents the absence of useful fruit: James invokes it to show that one cannot mix truths — "a fig tree cannot produce olives" (James 3:12) — for the very nature of the tree determines its fruit.
G4808.origine: The Greek word συκῆ comes from σῦκον (the fig, the fruit), forming a simple substantivized adjective that designates the tree that produces the fruit. In biblical Hebrew, the tree is called תְּאֵן (thééna), from a root possibly evoking abundance. It is a simple and direct word: the fig tree is primarily known by what it produces, like all trees in the Bible.
G4808.emploi: The word appears fifteen times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels. It is central to two major narratives: in Matthew and Mark, the cursing of the barren fig tree (21:19-21 and 11:13-21); in Luke, the parable of the fig tree planted in the vineyard (13:6-7), which speaks of a second chance given before judgment. Jesus also uses it as a natural symbol of discerning the times (Matthew 24:32, Mark 13:28, Luke 21:29). James uses it for a moral comparison: the tree reveals its nature. In Revelation (6:13), the fig trees are shaken as a sign of final judgment. Thus, the fig tree is less a simple plant than a biblical mirror of productivity, sterility, and judgment.
G4808.portee: The fig tree teaches two vital lessons. First, that our Christian life must be fruitful: having the Christian name is not enough; we must bear fruit (John 15:1-8). Second, that God discerns hypocrisy — false appearances hiding the absence of fruit — and calls for urgent repentance before judgment. It is an invitation to spiritual authenticity and action, not to hollow beautiful words.

sens: Eastern tree producing a coarse and wild fig, different from the common fig tree
Tree with low branches allowing easy climbing
G4809.detail:
1. The sycamore is a fruit tree native to the Mediterranean and Eastern regions, producing a fig of inferior quality compared to the true fig tree, but still edible. Its Greek name literally means "fig-mulberry," as it resembles both the fig tree and the mulberry. In Luke 19:4, it is on a sycamore that Zacchaeus climbs to see Jesus pass by, indicating that the tree has branches low enough and accessible for an adult man to climb without much difficulty.
2. The fact that Zacchaeus, a short man, was able to climb this tree to see Jesus shows that the sycamore does not require great agility to climb: its branches are naturally arranged to allow access, unlike some other taller trees.
G4809.origine: The Greek word συκομωραία is composed of σῦκον (fig) and μόρον (mulberry), which shows that the Greeks viewed this tree as a hybrid between the fig tree and the mulberry. It is a word borrowed from Eastern flora, used in the Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) to render the Hebrew שִׁקְמָה (chiqma), notably in Psalms 78:47 and Isaiah 9:10, where it is struck by the plagues of Egypt.
G4809.emploi: The word appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 19:4, in the account of the encounter between Jesus and Zacchaeus. Zacchaeus, chief tax collector of Jericho and a short man, is eager to see Jesus but cannot do so because of the crowd. He runs ahead and climbs a sycamore to see Him pass. This tree is specific to the region of Jericho, which is in a tropical zone, while Galilee further north, where Jesus primarily operates, does not have them.
G4809.portee: This brief mention of the sycamore reveals how Zacchaeus, despised as a tax collector, shows determination to meet Jesus: he overcomes both social disdain and his physical handicap (his short stature). The concrete detail of the tree anchors the scene in the reality of Jericho and shows that nothing can prevent someone who truly thirsts to meet the Lord.

sens: Fruit of the fig tree, generally golden or purple in color
Image of what is good and natural, product of a healthy tree
What reveals the true nature of a person or thing
Impossibility of obtaining a result contrary to the nature of a thing
G4810.detail:
1. The fig is the sweet and fleshy fruit of the fig tree, a common tree in the Holy Land. It is recognized by its oval shape and its flesh filled with small seeds. It is a nourishing and delicious food, symbolizing abundance.
2. In Jesus' teaching, the fig represents what is good and authentic, the natural fruit of a healthy tree. When He asks, "Do people pick grapes from thornbushes?" (Matthew 7:16), He uses the image of fruit to illustrate the impossible.
3. A good tree produces good fruit: the fig becomes the visible sign of what is hidden inside. That is why Jesus says that people are recognized "by their fruits" (Luke 6:44) — just as a fig tree is recognized by its figs.
4. The fig also serves to illustrate what cannot happen: a fig tree cannot produce olives, a vine cannot produce figs (James 3:12). What is naturally bad cannot produce good.
G4810.origine: The Greek word σῦκον comes from an ancient root that designates the fig tree and its fruit. In Hebrew, the Old Testament speaks of תְּאֵנָה (teéna, the fig), a tree highly cultivated in Israel. The fig tree was so common and valued that the fig becomes a strong biblical image: a symbol of prosperity, the promised land, and the true nature of things.
G4810.emploi: The word "fig" appears only four times in the Greek New Testament, always in the Synoptics and in James. Jesus uses it in His teaching about fruits: in Matthew 7:16 and Luke 6:44, He asks if figs can be picked from thornbushes or thistles, to show that each tree gives its own fruit — it is the sign of what comes from the heart. In Mark 11:13, the fig appears in the account of the barren fig tree, where Jesus looks for figs but finds only leaves. In James 3:12, the fig illustrates impossibility: a single source cannot produce both salty and fresh water, just as a fig tree cannot bear olives.
G4810.portee: For the believer, the fig teaches a simple yet profound lesson: one cannot hide who they truly are. Our actions, like the fruits of a tree, reveal the nature of our heart. Seeking a fig on a thistle is seeking good where only evil can grow. It is a call to examine our fruits — our life, our words, our choices — to verify what is truly growing within us.

sens: To steal from someone by trickery or threat, abusing one's power
To falsely accuse someone for personal gain
To harm someone by deceiving them
G4811.detail: 1. The original meaning is to steal by trickery or violence: one abuses their authority to extract money or goods from someone against their will. This is what Jesus forbids soldiers to do (Luke 3:14), who could easily coerce people into giving them money. 2. False accusation for profit is another aspect: one denounces someone without basis in order to gain money or personal satisfaction. 3. More broadly, it means to harm someone, causing damage through deception or abuse of authority. Zacchaeus acknowledges having acted this way (Luke 19:8) — he has harmed people, likely as a tax collector, by defrauding them.
G4811.origine: The word comes from a Greek expression that originally meant "to show a fig" (σῦκον = fig, φαίνω = to show). In Athens, it was an obscene act of insult; more broadly, it evoked denunciation and falsehood. Thus, the verb took on the meaning of "to falsely accuse" and finally "to extort, to steal by trickery." In Hebrew, it often translates עָשַׁק (to crush, to oppress) and other terms related to injustice and theft.
G4811.emploi: This verb appears twice in the New Testament, only in Luke. In both cases, it evokes serious dishonesty, an abuse of power or trust. Jesus commands soldiers not to extort, meaning not to steal from citizens by abusing their military authority. Zacchaeus, converted, acknowledges having extorted: as a tax collector, he took advantage of his position to plunder people. The verb emphasizes injustice, abuse of power, and deception.
G4811.portee: This word reminds us that Jesus firmly condemns all forms of theft, fraud, and abuse of power — whether one is a soldier, a leader, or a merchant. For the Christian, it is a call to absolute honesty: not to exploit the weak by taking advantage of one's authority or position. Zacchaeus' conversion shows that one who renounces extortion and makes amends becomes a friend of Jesus.

sens: To forcibly take someone to make them a prisoner or a slave
To divert someone from the truth by deceiving them
G4812.detail:
1. In the literal sense, the word evokes the action of war: to take someone away, to forcibly carry them off as booty that is captured. This is what happens to prisoners and captives taken during battles.
2. In a figurative sense, the term describes a deceptive seduction: someone tries to capture you, not by armed force, but by misleading you with false ideas. This is precisely what Paul denounces in Colossians 2:8: beware of being "captured" by those who offer you hollow philosophy instead of Christ. They make you a prisoner by diverting your mind from the truth.
G4812.origine: The Greek word combines two elements: "booty" (what is taken from the enemy) and "to lead, to carry" (ἄγω). The image is that of the victor who leads away his human booty. Paul uses it figuratively to show that false doctrines operate like a true spiritual kidnapping.
G4812.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Colossians 2:8. Paul uses it to warn Christians against the seductions of human philosophy that does not have Christ as its foundation. By choosing this martial and violent term, the apostle emphasizes the aggressive and dominating nature of erroneous ideas: they do not ask politely — they take, they capture, they enslave those who receive them without discernment.
G4812.portee: This word reminds believers that following a doctrine contrary to Christ is not simply choosing freely an opinion among others — it is allowing oneself to be captured, dominated, and enslaved. Paul invites vigilance: examining what is taught to us in the light of the Word and the person of Christ protects us against a spiritual captivity.

sens: To take away from someone what they possess, to steal or to plunder
To deprive someone of their resources or what they need
G4813.detail:
1. The word describes the action of taking someone's belongings, stealing or plundering them — like an enemy stripping a defeated foe. It is a brutal act where one takes what does not belong to them. In 2 Corinthians 11:8, Paul uses this word paradoxically: he says he has "stripped" other churches by accepting a salary from them, in order to serve the Corinthians for free — a strong image that shows how he accepted material help from other communities to avoid being a burden to the Corinthians.
2. More broadly, it means to deprive someone of their resources, of what they need. When Paul says he received from other churches ("stripping them"), he wants to show that he accepted support from elsewhere so as not to burden the budget of Corinth: it is an act of generosity on the part of those other churches.
G4813.origine: The word comes from Greek and expresses the idea of taking away, stripping. The root suggests the action of undressing or depriving someone of what they carry or possess. It is direct vocabulary, straightforward, reminiscent of acts of plunder or theft in antiquity.
G4813.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 11:8. Paul uses it in a context of tension with the Church of Corinth regarding the issue of his material support. He asserts that he never wanted to be a burden to the Corinthians, and for that, he accepted resources from other churches — hence the ironic use of the word "strip": he "plunders" others to spare Corinth. It is a rare word that adds emphasis to his argument.
G4813.portee: Paul uses this shocking image to show his love for the Corinthians: he accepted to be supported elsewhere rather than ask them for anything. It is a reminder of the generosity of the one who leads: being a pastor sometimes means accepting help from others to avoid burdening the sheep one serves. The text invites us to reflect on the material support of Gospel workers and the delicacy of service.

sens: To speak with someone, to have a conversation
To discuss a matter together, to consult each other
To deliberate, to make a decision together
G4814.detail:
1. To converse primarily refers to the act of speaking with someone, exchanging words: it is a conversation between two or more people. Moses and Elijah conversed with Jesus (Luke 9:30), meaning they talked together.
2. The word can also mean to discuss a specific matter, to come to an agreement on something. Judas went to confer with the chief priests about how to betray Jesus (Luke 22:4): there is a discussion to finalize a plan.
3. Finally, to converse can mean to deliberate together, to make a collective decision. Festus, after deliberating with the council, rendered his sentence (Acts 25:12): it is a consultation for an official decision.
G4814.origine: The word comes from the prefix *syn* ("with") combined with *laleō* ("to speak"). Literally, it means "to speak with." This root *laleō* is very active in New Testament Greek: it denotes concrete, ordinary speech, the kind exchanged simply. The compound reinforces the idea of exchange: one does not speak alone, but together.
G4814.emploi: The verb appears 6 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospels. It describes conversations: Moses and Elijah speaking with Jesus during the Transfiguration (Matthew 17:3, Mark 9:4, Luke 9:30); the disciples saying something to each other after a miracle (Luke 4:36). Twice, it has a nuance of consultation: Judas agreeing with the chief priests (Luke 22:4), and Festus deliberating with his council (Acts 25:12). The context gives the nuance: simple exchange or intentional discussion.
G4814.portee: This verb reminds us that communication is an important aspect of human and spiritual life. The great moments of faith — the Transfiguration — are marked by shared words. It also emphasizes that serious decisions often require collective reflection. It is a call to truly listen to one another, to seek together rather than alone.

sens: To stop, capture someone by force
To conceive a child, become pregnant
To come to someone's aid, assist someone
To gather, collect (in a literal sense)
To take, seize something
In a figurative sense: to give birth (to sin)
G4815.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to stop or capture a person, often with violence. It is to seize someone as a prisoner: the soldiers seized Jesus during his arrest (Luke 22:54, John 18:12).

2. For a woman, to conceive means to become pregnant, to carry a child in her womb. Elizabeth "became pregnant" after being barren (Luke 1:24), and the angel announces to Mary that she will "conceive" a son (Luke 1:36).

3. The word can also mean to come to someone's aid or assist someone in an action. Peter's companions come to "help" him pull in a net full of fish (Luke 5:7).

4. In a material context, it means to gather or collect things: the fishermen fill their boats with a great "catch" of fish (Luke 5:9).

5. Figuratively, the word describes how desire produces sin: lust "conceives" sin as a woman carries her child (James 1:15).
G4815.origine: The Greek word is composed of "syn" (together, with) and "lambanô" (to take, seize). The starting image is therefore "to take together" or "to take firmly." In the Old Testament translated into Greek, this word corresponds to the Hebrew "taphas" (to seize, take) and "harah" (to conceive). The preposition "syn" reinforces the idea: not only to take, but to take with force, uniting efforts.
G4815.emploi: This verb appears sixteen times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. The dominant meaning is "to seize" to stop a person: it is the verb chosen to describe the arrest of Jesus by the temple guards (Matthew 26:55, Luke 22:54, John 18:12) and that of Peter and John (Acts 12:3). Luke regularly uses the word for conception: Elizabeth conceives (1:24, 1:36), Mary will conceive (1:31), John in his mother's womb (2:21). The meaning "to help" is less frequent but clear (Luke 5:7, Philippians 4:3). A memorable image appears in James: desire "conceives" then "gives birth" to sin (1:15), like a living process of gestation.
G4815.portee: For the believer, this word shows how Jesus was arrested in a visible and brutal manner, a reality of his incarnation. The meaning of "to conceive" reminds us that human life begins in the mother's womb according to God's plan — a fundamental affirmation for understanding the dignity of the child. The image of desire that "conceives" sin helps to see evil not merely as a transgression, but as an inner birth: it grows within us before producing death. It is an invitation to monitor thoughts from their germination.

sens: To remove, take something from the ground or a place by pulling on it
To harvest, pick fruits or plants
To separate, isolate by removing from a whole
To take away, permanently remove
G4816.detail:
1. To tear out primarily means to remove something by pulling: it is to take a whole plant from the ground, roots and all. In the parable of the wheat and the tares, the servants want to tear out the weeds from the field (Matthew 13:28-29).

2. The verb also refers to the action of harvesting, picking: in Matthew 7:16 and Luke 6:44, one tears fruits from trees, that is, one picks them.

3. To tear out can mean to violently separate from a whole: in Matthew 13:41, the angels will tear out of the kingdom all causes of sin and those who do evil — they will remove them, isolating them from the people of God.

4. More broadly, to tear out expresses the idea of removing, taking away permanently: the tares are torn out and then thrown into the fire (Matthew 13:30, 13:40), they disappear.
G4816.origine: The Greek sullegō combines the prefix sun- ("with, together") and legō ("to gather, collect"). The basic image is therefore to gather, to put together by picking. In Hebrew, it primarily translates the verb laqat (לָקַט), which also means to gather, glean, pick. The Greek word emphasizes the action of taking, of uniting what is dispersed.
G4816.emploi: Sullegō appears 8 times, mainly in Matthew and Luke. Its biblical usage focuses on two areas: first agriculture (tearing out the weeds from the field, picking fruits), and then the more abstract action of removing or separating. In Matthew 13:28-41, the verb takes on a dramatic dimension — tearing out the tares is not a neutral gesture, it is to remove evil from good, a decisive separation. In Matthew 13:48, the good fish are gathered into containers. The eschatological context of Matthew 13:40-41 shows the verb used for the ultimate divine act: the angels will tear out the wicked definitively.
G4816.portee: This verb reminds the reader that God discerns good from evil and will act to separate them. The image of tearing out, violent and definitive, emphasizes that this separation is not symbolic or gentle: it is total and irreversible. For the believer, this invites a serious response to the call for purity and the reality of future judgment.

sens: To make a calculation, a count
To weigh arguments, seek an explanation
To discuss among oneself to reach a conclusion
G4817.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a calculation or count: to perform mental operations to arrive at a result. It is the idea of putting together (the prefix συλ- means "together") thoughts or numbers.
2. More broadly, the verb means to reason, that is, to weigh arguments and seek a logical explanation. In Luke 20:5, the chief priests "reasoned" among themselves, asking how to respond to Jesus' question about the baptism of John: they were calculating the consequences of each possible answer.
3. The verb also carries the idea of discussion: it is reasoning exchanged among several, where each contributes their reflection before arriving together at a conclusion.
G4817.origine: The word is composed of the prefix συλ- ("together") and λογίζομαι ("to count, calculate"). It evokes the image of gathering thoughts or elements to draw a conclusion. The root logos (word, reason) reminds us that to reason is to make use of reason. In Hebrew, it often translates חָשַׁב (hashab), which means to count, think, or meditate.
G4817.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Luke 20:5. It is a scene where the chief priests, scribes, and elders pose a tricky question about the origin of John's baptism. Unable to answer without compromising themselves, they reason among themselves, mentally weighing what it is prudent to say. It is a moment where human reasoning stumbles upon pride and the fear of losing authority.
G4817.portee: This word reminds us that reasoning is not neutral: one always reasons based on their interests and fears. The Jewish leaders reason, but not to seek the truth — rather to protect themselves. The believer is invited to examine their own reasoning: does it serve to know God, or to justify their refusal to obey Him?

sens: To feel sadness or sorrow by sharing the feelings of another person
To be moved with compassion in the face of another's suffering or misfortune
G4818.detail:
1. The word describes a sadness that arises from solidarity with someone else: one suffers because the other suffers. It is an emotion of deep sympathy, a participation in the pain or mourning. In Mark 3:5, Jesus is saddened to see the hardness of heart of the men who are watching him.

2. More broadly, it means to be moved with compassion, to be touched by the misery or misfortune of a person. It is the opposite of indifference: the heart resonates with someone else's difficult situation, and this resonance provokes a true inner sorrow.
G4818.origine: The word is composed of two elements: the preposition « συν » (with) and the verb « λυπέω » (to sadden, to cause pain). This composition clearly indicates that the pain comes from sharing: one does not suffer alone, but with someone. The initial image is that of a sadness that is common, shared, which unites the one who feels it to the one who is its object.
G4818.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 3:5. Jesus has just healed a man with a withered hand, but he encounters the opposition of the Pharisees. The evangelist Matthew reports that Jesus, "looking around at them with anger," is at the same time "grieved" by their spiritual hardness. This passage reveals the two emotions of Christ: a holy indignation at evil, and a true sorrow at the voluntary refusal of those who do not want to recognize him. The word emphasizes that this affliction is not cold or distant, but deeply human, driven by compassion.
G4818.portee: This verb shows that Christ is not indifferent to the hardness of the human heart. His indignation is accompanied by authentic affliction: he suffers with those who are lost by their refusal. For the reader, it is a call to cultivate this compassion in their own relationships: not to judge coldly those who stray, but to suffer with them, share their condition, and pray for them. It is also a comfort: Jesus does not distance himself from the sinner; he looks at them with sorrow and love.

sens: To stand together, to be gathered
To come to an agreement, to agree
To occur, to take place, to happen
G4819.detail:
1. The primary meaning of the word, very concrete, evokes the image of feet coming closer, of people standing together or converging — an idea of gathering or physical meeting.

2. From this image arises the meaning of agreeing or concluding an agreement: when people come together to discuss, it results in an arrangement, a mutual consent.

3. The main meaning in the New Testament is "to occur" or "to happen": an event that arrives, that manifests. This is how Jesus announces to his disciples what "must happen to him" (Mark 10:32), or how the disciples discuss "everything that had happened" in Jerusalem (Luke 24:14). The word designates both the trials that arise — "the trials that [were] brought upon me by the plots of the Jews" (Acts 20:19) — and the astonishing miracles: "what [had] happened" to the healed beggar (Acts 3:10). It always refers to events that come into existence, that occur, whether they are joyful or painful.
G4819.origine: The word is composed of the particle « syn » (with) and the verb « baïnô » (to walk, to advance). The basic image is therefore that of one who walks with others, who goes together. This composition reflects the idea of convergence: the events that "happen" converge towards us, they occur to us. The word translates in the Greek Old Testament verbs such as « asah » (to do), « karah » (to meet, to happen) or « qara » (to call, to occur), showing that the Greeks saw in « symbainô » the natural equivalent of these Hebrew expressions to say that something occurs.
G4819.emploi: The verb appears about 8 times in the New Testament, mainly in Acts and in the epistles. It always expresses the idea that an event is realized or occurs. In Luke (Gospel and Acts), it designates the facts that take place: what happens to Jesus (Mark 10:32), what happened during his passion (Luke 24:14), or what happens to the apostles — a healed beggar (Acts 3:10), persecutions (Acts 20:19), a commotion (Acts 21:35). Peter and Paul use it to invite believers to see trials not as strange surprises, but as realities that the Lord ordains. The word emphasizes the certain, real, and inevitable nature of what happens: these are not rumors or assumptions, but events that truly occur.
G4819.portee: This word reminds believers that the events of their lives — joys, persecutions, trials — are not accidents or absurdities. They "happen," they truly occur, often with hidden divine wisdom. Peter exhorts believers not to be "surprised as though something strange were happening" by sufferings (1 Peter 4:12), suggesting that what happens is part of God's design. The word invites a clear faith, which recognizes realities and expects God to act — or to allow things to happen — according to his will.

sens: To think, to meditate, to turn over in one's mind
To discuss, to debate, to converse together
To meet, to join someone
To be useful, to contribute to someone's good
G4820.detail:
1. To think deeply about something, turning it over in one's mind like one turns a ball from hand to hand. This is what Mary does after the birth of Jesus: she "reflects" on all the wonderful events in her heart, keeping and meditating on them continually (Luke 2:19). The image suggests a gentle, repeated reflection that seeks to understand.
2. To discuss, to debate together — literally "to throw words together." When the apostles Peter and John are released by the Sanhedrin, the members "deliberate" among themselves about what to do (Acts 4:15). It is a serious discussion, where each person contributes their words to the group.
3. To meet, to come to meet someone. Paul "joins" his traveling companions at Assos after taking a walk (Acts 20:14). The word carries the simple idea of convergence, of crossing paths.
4. To be useful, to contribute positively. Apollos, after his visit to the believers in Achaia, proves to be very "useful" to those who had believed, helping them in their faith (Acts 18:27). It is to bring something beneficial to someone.
G4820.origine: The word is composed of two elements: « syn » (together) and « ballô » (to throw). The basic image is therefore "to throw together." This root « ballô » has given rise to many words in Greek: « balle » (a ball for play), « problème » (what is thrown before oneself as an obstacle), « parabol » (parable, what is thrown alongside for comparison). The ancient meaning of "to throw together" has naturally expanded: to throw words together = to discuss, to turn an idea together in one's heart = to meditate, to converge together = to meet.
G4820.emploi: The verb « sumballô » appears 6 times in the New Testament, almost always in the Gospel of Luke and in Acts. In Luke, it describes the action of Mary who meditates (Luke 2:19), that of a king who reflects on war (Luke 14:31). In Acts, it is mostly found in apostolic dialogues: the apostles deliberate (4:15), philosophers converse with Paul (17:18), Paul meets his companions (20:14). A particular form, the middle form, appears in Acts 18:27 with the meaning of "to contribute" or "to be useful." The word always retains a nuance of shared action or interaction between several people or thoughts.
G4820.portee: This word shows us the biblical importance of inner meditation (like Mary who reflects on the events of Jesus' life) and of honest dialogue in the Christian community. It reminds us that our faith grows when we deeply reflect on God's acts and when we build each other up through words. It is a call not to remain superficial, but to "reflect" in our hearts on what God accomplishes.

sens: Exercising royal authority together with someone
Sharing power and glory in a common reign
Participating in the victory and triumph of a king
G4821.detail:
1. This verb expresses the idea of reigning together, governing side by side with a king or leader. It is a shared authority, not isolated. In 1 Corinthians 4:8, Paul ironically tells the Corinthians: "without us you have begun to reign," implying that they would fully reign "with us" if their glory were authentic.
2. The word especially emphasizes union, communion in power and honor. It is a reign of two or in a group, not a solitary reign. In 2 Timothy 2:12, Paul promises: "if we endure, we will also reign with him [Christ]," showing that faithful believers will share in the glorious kingship of the risen Christ.
3. By extension, the word evokes participation in the final victory and dignity of the eternal reign. It is less about concrete political power than about a future exaltation alongside Christ.
G4821.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "συν" (sun, "with") and "βασιλεύω" (basileuō, "to reign"). The root "βασιλ-" (basil-) comes from ancient Greek and means "king," an image of power and sovereign authority. This compound clearly expresses the idea of sharing, of communion in the exercise of royal power.
G4821.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times by Paul. In 1 Corinthians 4:8, it is used ironically: Paul reproaches the Corinthians for thinking they are already kings, without him and his companions. In 2 Timothy 2:12, it takes on a positive and eschatological (future-oriented) meaning: it is a promise that faithful believers will reign with Christ in his eternal glory. The context thus shifts from critical irony to an exhortation of hope.
G4821.portee: This promise transforms the Christian's perspective on present suffering. Paul says: if you endure now, you will reign with Christ in glory. It is an encouragement to remain faithful in difficult days. The word reminds us that faith is not just an internal matter, but a participation in the final victory of Christ and his eternal honor.

sens: Join, assemble parts to form a coherent whole
Compare, examine together to draw a conclusion
Demonstrate, prove by reasoning
Teach, instruct by transmitting knowledge
G4822.detail:
1. To join or assemble: this is the most concrete meaning. The different parts of the body of Christ, connected by joints and ligaments, are "firmly joined together" (Colossians 2:19) and "form a solid assembly" (Ephesians 4:16) — the image is that of a living body where each element holds together harmoniously. The believers themselves are "united in love" (Colossians 2:2), forming a communion.

2. To compare to conclude: this means putting together several elements to deduce a conclusion. After his vision, Paul "concluded" that the Lord was calling him to Macedonia (Acts 16:10) — he examined the circumstances and drew certainty from them. It is reasoning that leads to a decision.

3. To demonstrate: this means proving something through a logical sequence. Saul "demonstrates" that Jesus is the Christ (Acts 9:22) by providing evidence and tight arguments. The term implies a work of the mind that brings the truth to light.

4. To teach: this means transmitting knowledge by forming the mind. No one can "instruct" the mind of the Lord (1 Corinthians 2:16) — it is impossible to teach him anything. Elsewhere, it is the task of teachers to "instruct" the disciples, guiding them step by step.
G4822.origine: The word is composed of "syn" (together) and "bibazô" (to make walk, lead, establish); the latter comes from the verb "baïnô" which means "to go" or "to ascend." The basic idea is thus "to make go together" or "to assemble by leading towards." In the Greek of the Old Testament, it mainly translates verbs of teaching or direction: "to teach" (Hebrew "yarah," to show the way), "to make known" (Hebrew "yada"), "to give discernment" (Hebrew "bin").
G4822.emploi: This verb appears seven times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul and Luke. In Luke (Acts), it mainly means "to conclude" or "to demonstrate": Saul demonstrates the messiahship of Jesus (Acts 9:22), Paul concludes that God is calling him to Macedonia (Acts 16:10). In Paul's epistles, the meaning shifts towards "to unite" or "to assemble": the body of Christ is made up of members "united" and "firmly assembled" by joints (Colossians 2:2, 2:19; Ephesians 4:16). One occurrence seems to have the meaning of "to instruct" (1 Corinthians 2:16). Thus, the word covers both a mental operation (reasoning, concluding) and a physical or ecclesial operation (assembling, uniting).
G4822.portee: This word reminds the believer of two essential truths. First, that the Church is a living body where each member, linked to others, contributes to the growth and solidity of the whole: one cannot live their faith in isolation. Second, that Christian thought must reason from the Word and Revelation: to know Jesus is to be able to demonstrate who he is, not through sterile reasoning, but through the logical sequence of facts and divine promise.

sens: To give advice to someone, to exhort them to act in a certain way
To recommend an action, a decision, a plan
To come to an agreement with others to deliberate together, to consult
To seek someone's opinion, to consult them
G4823.detail:
1. To counsel someone means to tell them what one thinks they should do. In Revelation 3:18, the Lord advises the believer in Laodicea to buy refined gold to become spiritually rich: it is a benevolent counsel, a personal recommendation.

2. To recommend a measure or decision means to propose it as being good. In John 18:14, Caiaphas gave this counsel to the Jews that it was advantageous for one man to die for the people: the word designates the advice given in a serious matter.

3. To consult means to hold counsel together, to come to an agreement after discussion. In Acts 9:23, the Jews conspired to kill Paul: several people discuss a project together and decide to act in concert.

4. To consult means to seek someone's opinion before acting. In Matthew 26:4, the chief priests and elders deliberated on how to arrest Jesus: they held counsel, exchanging ideas to agree on a plan.
G4823.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek σύν (syn, "with") and βουλή (boulè, "counsel, deliberation"). It evokes the idea of shared reflection, of a concerted will. In classical Greek, it first means "to hold counsel with," then "to give advice to" someone. The root evokes will and deliberate judgment.
G4823.emploi: The verb appears four times in the New Testament. In Matthew 26:4, Jesus' adversaries deliberate together on a malicious plan. In John 18:14, it designates the counsel given publicly and solemnly by Caiaphas, the high priest. In Acts 9:23, the Jews conspire again, this time against Paul. In Revelation 3:18, the risen Lord directly advises the believer, in a tone of tenderness and exhortation. The word thus shifts from hostile deliberation (the enemies of God) to benevolent recommendation (Jesus towards his people). It always designates serious, weighed reflection, never a trivial or improvised counsel.
G4823.portee: This word reminds us that important decisions require deliberation and counsel. It shows how men conspire, sometimes for evil (against Jesus, against Paul), but also how Jesus himself advises us with authority and kindness. For the Christian, it is an invitation to seek the counsel of God and his people rather than to act alone in impulsiveness.

sens: Deliberation among several people on an important subject
Advice or recommendations given to decide an action
Assembly or group of people gathered to deliberate
G4824.detail:
1. The word primarily describes the action of deliberating together, discussing to make a decision. When the Pharisees "hold counsel" against Jesus (Matthew 27:1), they gather to examine how to make him perish: this is a collective deliberation.
2. It can also refer to the advice or plan that results from it: "after deliberating," the Jewish leaders decide to buy a field with the traitor's money (Matthew 27:7). Here, the counsel is the decision itself.
3. By extension, the word can name the group or assembly that deliberates, as indicated in Acts 25:12 where Paul appeals to the "counsel" of Caesar.
G4824.origine: The word comes from σύμβουλος (sumboulos), which means "one who deliberates with someone," composed of σύν (syn, "with") and βουλή (boulè, "will, deliberation"). It is a word from the spoken and written Greek of the Greco-Roman period, corresponding to the Latin consilium. The root suggests the idea of sharing one's thoughts to decide together.
G4824.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the New Testament, mostly in Matthew. It generally refers to the deliberation of Jewish religious authorities seeking to harm Jesus: the Pharisees "consult" (Matthew 12:14, 22:15), the Jewish leaders "hold counsel" to condemn him (Matthew 27:1, 28:12). Mark uses the same word (3:6, 15:1). In all these cases, it is a malicious concertation. Only once, in Acts 25:12, the term designates the imperial council of the Roman emperor, showing that the word can also name an official institution.
G4824.portee: This word reveals how Jesus' adversaries acted: not through isolated action, but through collective calculation and prior deliberation. For the Christian, this shows that the passion of Christ was not an accident, but the result of a conscious human strategy — which makes Jesus' submission to his death even more voluntary and significant. It is also a reminder that God's truth disturbs those who have interests to defend.

sens: Person who gives advice and recommendations
One who participates in the deliberations of an authority
In a figurative sense: one who shares the thoughts or secrets of an important person
G4825.detail:
1. A counselor is a person whose advice and recommendations are sought regarding decisions to be made. It is someone trustworthy whom one relies on to discern what is good.

2. The word can also refer to one who sits alongside an authority (a king, a magistrate) to deliberate with them and participate in their decisions. They then have an official role.

3. In a figurative and deeper sense, it is one who knows and shares the intimate thoughts of an important person — notably of God. In Romans 11:34, Paul asks: "Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?" — that is, who has ever had access to God's secrets to guide or correct him?
G4825.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: σύν (sun, "with") and βουλή (boulè, "deliberation, counsel"). A counselor is literally "one who deliberates with." In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it translates יָעַץ (ya'ats), "to give advice, consult," found in contexts of wisdom and governance. The image is one of shared reflection, of participation in the thoughts of others.
G4825.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament in Romans 11:34, where Paul cites Isaiah 40:13 to affirm God's absolute transcendence. No creature, no angel, no wise person can be God's counselor, for no one knows his thoughts nor has the right to guide him. It is an affirmation of divine uniqueness and sovereignty: God needs no one and is accountable to no one. The usage thus underscores God's absolute incomparability compared to human authorities.
G4825.portee: This word invites the reader to recognize God's absolute wisdom and independence. If no one can be God's counselor, it is because his thoughts infinitely surpass ours and we should never presume to correct him or impose our ideas on him. This calls for humility and trust: we can rely on a God who needs no one and sees all.

sens: Pious and aged man who was waiting for the consolation of Israel
One who recognizes Jesus as a child in the Temple as the promised Messiah
G4826G.detail:
1. Simeon is a faithful man of Israel, righteous and devout, living in Jerusalem at the time of Jesus' birth. The Holy Spirit was upon him, and he was faithfully waiting for the coming of the Messiah, called "the consolation of Israel" (Luke 2:25). His name, Hebrew, means "one who has heard" or "one who listens."

2. Simeon plays a crucial role in the Gospel of Luke: he recognizes in the child Jesus presented at the Temple the long-awaited Messiah. He blesses the family and prophesies to Mary that a "sword of sorrow" will pierce her soul, for this child will be "a sign of contradiction" — some will reject him, others will believe (Luke 2:34). He embodies the patient waiting of the chosen people and the yes of faith that recognizes God at work.
G4826G.origine: The name Simeon comes from the Hebrew שִׁמְעוֹן (Shimʿôn), whose root means "to listen" or "to hear." It evokes one who listens to God and welcomes his word. In Greek, this name is also written Σίμων (Simôn), a shorter form, but Συμεών (Sumeōn) is the more literal transliteration of the Hebrew. The name appears in the Old Testament for one of Jacob's sons (Genesis 29:33).
G4826G.emploi: The New Testament designates several different characters by the name Simeon, but in the Gospel of Luke (2:25, 34), it exclusively refers to this righteous and devout old man who was waiting for "the consolation of Israel." According to the account, the Holy Spirit had warned him that he would not see death before he had seen the Messiah. When Jesus' parents present him at the Temple, according to the Law, Simeon suddenly recognizes him as the long-awaited Messiah. He blesses the child and the mother, revealing that the child will be a cause of falling and rising for many in Israel, and that this event will provoke contradiction. His role in Luke emphasizes that even before Jesus' death and resurrection, faithful souls, guided by the Spirit, already recognized him as the Savior.
G4826G.portee: The figure of Simeon encourages the believer in patient waiting and faithfulness. He waited his whole life for the coming of the Messiah, undoubtedly without seeing spectacular fulfillments, but remaining righteous and devout, filled with the Holy Spirit. His example shows that true consolation comes from the certainty that God will fulfill his promises. Moreover, his prophecy reveals that faith in Jesus will not bring a false easy peace, but division: some will reject him, others will follow him. It is a call to welcome Jesus clearly, knowing that he transforms and judges at the same time.

sens: Ancestor of Jesus, son of Judah in the genealogy of Luke
G4826H.detail: 1. Simeon is a man listed in the genealogy of Jesus according to the Gospel of Luke. He is the son of Judah and the father of Joseph (or Jonam according to the manuscripts): Luke 3:30 places him in this chain of ancestors that traces back from Jesus to Adam. This character belongs to the post-exilic period of Israel's history, many centuries after King David.
G4826H.origine: The name Simeon comes from the Hebrew Shiméon (שִׁמְעוֹן), which literally means "God has heard" or "one who listens." It carries the idea that God answers prayers. It is a name rooted in Jewish faith, once borne by Jacob's first son (Genesis 29:33), whose tribe Simeon was one of the twelve tribes of Israel. In Greek, this name is sometimes written Sumeōn (Συμεών) and sometimes Simōn (Σίμων), two forms that coexist in the New Testament.
G4826H.emploi: Simeon appears in the genealogy of Jesus in Luke 3:30 as a link in the genealogical chain that establishes that Jesus, legal son of Joseph, descends from David and Abraham. Luke methodically lists Joseph's ancestors to show that Jesus is fully part of the history of the Jewish people and the messianic promises.
G4826H.portee: This mention of Simeon in the genealogy of Jesus reminds the reader that Jesus does not appear out of nowhere: he has a history, ancestors, a place rooted in the people of Israel. It is a detail that reinforces the incarnation — the Son of God is rooted in concrete humanity.

sens: son of Jacob and Leah
ancestor of Christ
pious elder who recognized Jesus in the temple
prophet from Antioch nicknamed Niger
another name for the disciple Peter
G4826I.detail:
1. Simeon is one of the twelve sons of Jacob, born of his first wife Leah (Genesis 29:33). He is an important figure in the Old Testament, founder of one of the twelve tribes of Israel. In Revelation, the tribe of Simeon is mentioned among the twelve who receive the seal of God (Revelation 7:7).

2. A Simeon is also listed as an ancestor of Jesus in his genealogy, situated in the line of David according to the Gospel of Luke (Luke 3:30).

3. It is also the name of the pious elder who was waiting for the consolation of Israel in the temple of Jerusalem (Luke 2:25, 34). Filled with the Holy Spirit, he recognizes the child Jesus as the promised Messiah and takes him in his arms, pronouncing a famous blessing.

4. A prophet named Simeon, nicknamed Niger (meaning "the Black"), is mentioned as one of the teachers of the Church in Antioch alongside Barnabas and Saul (Acts 13:1).

5. The name Simeon also refers to the apostle Peter, who is sometimes called by this Hebrew name rather than by his Greek equivalent Σίμων (Acts 15:14, 2 Peter 1:1).
G4826I.origine: Simeon comes from the Hebrew שִׁמְעוֹן (Shimʿon), whose root literally means "he has heard" or "one who listens." This name was common in Israel and had a strong biblical resonance. In Greek, the name is written in two ways: Συμεών (Sumeōn), closer to the Hebrew pronunciation, and Σίμων (Simōn), more Hellenized. Both forms refer to the same characters.
G4826I.emploi: Συμεών appears about 5 times in the New Testament to designate five distinct characters. In the Gospels, it names the pious elder of the temple (Luke 2-3) and an ancestor of Jesus. In Acts, it refers to a prophet from Antioch (Acts 13:1) and sometimes to the apostle Peter (Acts 15:14). The context always indicates which Simeon is being referred to: the context of the temple, the genealogy, the Church of Antioch, or the apostleship. This diversity of characters shows that it was a very common name among the Jews.
G4826I.portee: For the Christian reader, the Simeon of the temple embodies the patient and humble expectation of the divine promise: filled with the Holy Spirit, he discerns in the child Jesus the fulfillment of the messianic promises. His example shows that true faith recognizes Christ even in the humble appearance of a newborn. The other Simeons also remind us that the Gospel is deeply rooted in the history of Israel and is addressed to those who, like the old Simeon, genuinely seek God.

sens: Son of Jacob and Leah in the Old Testament
Ancestor of Jesus in his genealogy
Pious elder who recognized Jesus in the Temple
Prophet and teacher of the church in Antioch
Name given to the apostle Peter
G4826J.detail:
1. Simeon is a fundamental character of the Old Testament: he is the second son of Jacob and Leah. His name means "God has heard" in Hebrew. A tribe of Israel bears his name and is among the twelve tribes of the chosen people (Revelation 7:7 mentions this tribe in the vision of the one hundred forty-four thousand elect).

2. As an ancestor of Jesus, Simeon appears in the genealogy of the Messiah (Luke 3:30), showing that Jesus descends from the line of Jacob.

3. A man named Simeon, now aged and righteous, was waiting for the Messiah in the Temple of Jerusalem. The Holy Spirit revealed to him that he would see the Christ before his death, and he recognized Jesus during his presentation at the Temple (Luke 2:25-34), pronouncing a prophetic word about the child's and his mother's fate.

4. Simeon the Niger (meaning "Simeon the Black") was a prophet and teacher in Antioch, among the first leaders of the nascent church (Acts 13:1).

5. Simeon is also the name given to the apostle Peter, particularly in the epistles (2 Peter 1:1 and Acts 15:14), recalling his original Hebrew identity.
G4826J.origine: The name Simeon comes from the Hebrew שִׁמְעוֹן (Shimèon), composed of שׁמע (shamah, "to hear") and the suffix -ōn, which literally means "he has heard" or "God has heard." In Greek, this name has two main forms: Συμεών (Sumeōn) and Σίμων (Simon). The form Συμεών is closer to the original Hebrew pronunciation and is often used to emphasize the Jewish identity of the person.
G4826J.emploi: Simeon designates several important biblical characters. The earliest is the son of Jacob mentioned in the Old Testament, whose tribe remained one of the twelve tribes of Israel until the exile. In the New Testament, the name reappears across generations: first as an ancestor of Jesus (Luke 3:30), then as the pious elder of the Temple who blesses Jesus (Luke 2:25-34), then as Simeon Niger, prophet of the church in Antioch (Acts 13:1), and finally as the apostle Peter himself, called Simeon in formal passages (2 Peter 1:1). The persistence of this name through generations reflects its importance in Jewish piety and in the history of salvation.
G4826J.portee: For the Christian, Simeon the elder of the Temple embodies the patient expectation of God's promise. His story shows that the Holy Spirit guides those who sincerely seek Christ and that patience in faith will find its fulfillment. The apostle Peter, bearing the same name, reminds us that Jesus called ordinary men to be the pillars of his church. These narratives together testify to the continuity of God's covenant from the people of Israel to the new Church.

sens: Apostle of Jesus Christ, initially called Simon
The first of the twelve apostles, who received the name Peter
G4826K.detail: Simon Peter is the full name of one of the twelve apostles of Jesus. In the provided passages, he is simply referred to as "Simon" (Acts 15:14, where Simon reports how God chose from the nations a people bearing his name; 2 Peter 1:1, where he introduces himself as "Simon Peter, servant and apostle of Jesus Christ"). He is the same man that the New Testament also calls Cephas or Peter (in Greek Σίμων/Sîmôn), to whom Jesus entrusted a special role in the Church.
G4826K.origine: Συμεών comes from the Hebrew שִׁמְעוֹן (Shim'ôn), which means "one who listens" or "listens." This name is rooted in the Old Testament: it was originally the name of the second son of Jacob and Leah (Genesis 29:33). The New Testament uses both the Hebrew form Συμεών and its Greek variant Σίμων (Sîmôn). These two forms refer to the same person depending on the context and manuscripts.
G4826K.emploi: In the New Testament, Συμεών appears mainly in two later passages where the apostle is referred to by his Hebrew name: Acts 15:14, during the Jerusalem council, where Peter (called "Simon" there) speaks to testify to God's choice regarding the nations; and 2 Peter 1:1, at the opening of the second epistle, where the apostle signs by combining his Hebrew name and his Greek nickname "Simon Peter." This Hebrew form is less frequent than the Greek form Σίμων, but it emphasizes the Jewish identity and Hebrew roots of the apostle.
G4826K.portee: Simon Peter embodies the ordinary apostle whom Jesus chose and transformed. His name "one who listens" reminds us of the importance of listening to God's word and obeying it. The fact that the New Testament uses both his Hebrew name and the nickname "Peter" that Jesus gave him shows how God changes and uses those who follow him: from Simon the fragile fisherman, he made Peter the rock on which he would build his Church.

sens: A disciple who shares the teaching of the same master with others
G4827.detail: 1. A condisciple is a disciple who learns alongside other disciples from the same master. The Greek word combines "with" and "disciple": it refers to one who studies together with peers. In John 11:16, Thomas addresses the other apostles in this way, recognizing that they are all disciples of Jesus together and share the same mission and fate.
G4827.origine: The word comes from the Greek root μανθάνω (to learn) preceded by the prefix σύν (with). This is why it is said "condisciple" in French: "con-" also means "with." The word designates one who learns "with" their companions, under the same authority.
G4827.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in John 11:16. Thomas uses it to address his fellow apostles when Jesus wants to return to Judea where he is threatened. By calling the others "condisciples," Thomas shows that he sees himself and them as a united group, bound by the same learning from Jesus and sharing the same commitment, even to the point of dying together.
G4827.portee: This word reminds us that the apostles are not isolated disciples, but a community of supportive learners. For the Christian, it illustrates that faith in Jesus is lived out in a fraternal communion with other believers, all equally disciples of the same master. Thomas uses it to reinforce the unity of the group in the face of danger.

sens: To testify together, to provide a common proof
To confirm by one's own testimony
To support or validate the testimony of another
To bear inner witness from the Spirit
G4828.detail:
1. This verb literally means "to testify with," like two or more witnesses who speak together to establish a truth. Conscience "bears witness" with or alongside the law of God written in the heart: it confirms that this law is real and just (Romans 2:15).
2. The word also designates the moment when something internal confirms what we believe: the Spirit of God "bears witness with our spirit" that we are children of God, our own feeling uniting with the cry of the Spirit himself (Romans 8:16).
3. It is also the act of swearing, solemnly certifying what one asserts: Paul swears "in Christ" and calls upon his conscience to testify to his absolute sincerity (Romans 9:1).
4. In all cases, the verb evokes a concordance, a union of inner voices that together validate a divine truth.
G4828.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "syn" (with) and "martureō" (to testify, to bear witness). The simple verb "martureō" comes from a root designating the witness; it evokes the idea of memory, of remembrance, of recalling the past. In Hebrew, the corresponding root is "ʿēd" (witness), which also suggests the idea of visible proof, a monument that speaks. The prefix "syn" transforms the action into a concordance, a shared validation.
G4828.emploi: This verb appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the letter to the Romans. In Romans 2:15, the conscience of the Gentiles "bears witness" with the law written in their hearts, thus validating divine judgment. In Romans 8:16, it is the Holy Spirit himself who "bears witness with our spirit," creating an inner harmony that assures the believer of their adoption. In Romans 9:1, Paul uses the verb solemnly to swear on his conscience and the Spirit that he is telling the truth. The central meaning is always a double validation: two witnesses or two forces that unite to confirm a truth.
G4828.portee: This word shows us that faith is not isolated: it is rooted in a deep inner concordance. When the Spirit bears witness to our spirit, we are not left alone with our doubts; a harmony arises between our regenerated conscience and the Spirit of God. This verb also reminds us that God respects our dignity: He does not impose Himself; He testifies with us, attesting to a reality that we can also recognize from within.

sens: To share something with others, to receive a portion
To enjoy together a common advantage or benefit
G4829.detail:
1. The verb literally means "to divide into parts" or "to share." It describes the action of receiving a portion of a good, a resource, or a privilege distributed. In 1 Corinthians 9:13, Paul uses this concrete image: those who serve at the altar "have part in the altar," meaning they receive a portion of the offerings presented there — it is their right and their sustenance.

2. In a figurative sense, the verb describes the act of enjoying together a common advantage or a shared blessing. It is to participate in what belongs to a community or a function. The image remains that of a legitimate share, a portion that rightfully belongs to the one who receives it.
G4829.origine: The Greek word is composed of the prefix συν (syn, "with") and the verb μερίζω (merizō, "to divide into parts," itself derived from μέρος, méros, "part"). This root μέρος appears in many Greek words related to sharing and portion. The verb also appears, without the prefix, in the Greek translations of the Old Testament (LXX), notably to translate the Hebrew חָלַק (halaq, "to share, to divide"), which appears in Proverbs 29:24. The composition with συν adds the idea of "sharing with" or "having part together."
G4829.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 9:13, in the context where Paul defends the right of the apostles to be supported by the Church. He uses this phrase to establish a biblical parallel: just as the priests of the Old Testament had the right to "share" in the offerings of the altar (to have part in the portions reserved for worship), so too do the workers of the Gospel have the right to be materially supported by those they serve. The verb expresses here an established right, a participation that is self-evident in the order of things.
G4829.portee: This passage teaches that one who dedicates their energy to religious or spiritual service has the right to live from it. For a Christian, this establishes the principle of fair compensation for those who dedicate themselves to ministry. It is also a lesson in equity: one who works for a common good should not be left in poverty. Beyond that, it speaks of the sharing of graces and blessings within the faith community.

sens: To have a share together in something
To be associated with something in an indissoluble manner
To share a common community or condition
G4830.detail: 1. The word designates the act of having a share or portion in something in common with others. In Ephesians 3:6, the Gentiles "participate in the same promise" made to Israel: they are not simply included, they truly receive the same inheritance and blessing as believing Jews. It is a complete equality in what is received. 2. The word can also mean to be associated or complicit with someone in an action or condition. In Ephesians 5:7, Paul commands Christians to have no "part" with those who live in sin: it is about not being mixed with their evil works, to remain separate. This is a communion to avoid, unlike the first sense where it is a precious communion to embrace.
G4830.origine: The word is formed from the prefix "syn-" (together, with) and "métochos" (one who shares, who has a part). The root "mét-" comes from the verb meaning "to have a share in." In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears to translate notions of inheritance and common sharing. It is a word that emphasizes the "with" dimension: sharing is never alone, it is always together with others.
G4830.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the letter to the Ephesians. In Ephesians 3:6, it describes the central revelation of God's plan: the Gentiles become "fellow heirs" with Israel, entering into the same promise made to the patriarchs. It is an image of radical equality and inclusion in the family of God. In Ephesians 5:7, the same word takes on a negative connotation: Paul uses the verb in the negative imperative to prohibit a "participation" in the unfruitful works of darkness. The context changes, but the fundamental meaning remains: to share something "with." Paul uses this word to express the gravest idea in Christian ethics — being associated, identified with someone or something — hence the importance of choosing one's associations wisely.
G4830.portee: This word highlights a crucial truth for the Christian: in Jesus Christ, all believers — Jews and Gentiles alike — inherit together the same divine promises. But it also reminds us that this precious communion requires moral vigilance from us. We cannot simultaneously be "participants" in the life of Christ and maintain a "part" with darkness. The word calls the Christian to a coherence of life: if I am truly associated with Christ, I must be fully so.

sens: one who imitates with others
one who follows the example of a person in communion with other believers
