G4831.detail: 1. The word literally designates someone who imitates in the company of others, who shares the imitation of the same model. Paul uses this term in Philippians 3:17 to invite believers to collectively imitate his example and that of his companions: "Be all my imitators, brothers." 2. On a spiritual level, it is the idea of following together the same model of Christian life. Imitation is not solitary but communal: believers encourage each other by walking in the same footsteps of those who faithfully live the Gospel.
G4831.origine: The word is formed from the prefix "syn" (with) and "mimètès" (one who imitates), itself derived from "mimeomai" (to imitate). This composition emphasizes the collective and fraternal aspect of imitation: one does not follow a model alone, but in the company of other believers who share the same commitment.
G4831.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 3:17. Paul uses it to exhort the Philippians to collectively imitate him and his brothers in Christ who live according to the example of Christ. This context shows that Christian imitation is a communal act: believers support one another in following together the footsteps of those who walk faithfully.
G4831.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that following Christ is not an isolated endeavor, but a shared adventure. The Church is a community of imitators who encourage one another to walk as Jesus walked. Seeing how others live faith faithfully is a grace and a call to grow together in resemblance to Christ.

sens: Having the same form, the same appearance
Conforming to a model, made identical by transformation
Adapted to, harmonized with
G4832.detail: 1. The primary meaning is that of a resemblance in form or outward appearance: two similar things have the same figure. This is the concrete sense of the word. 2. But the Bible uses this word for a deeper resemblance: that of a transformation brought about by the power of God. In Philippians 3:21, Christ "will transform the body of our humiliation, making it similar to the body of his glory" — this refers to a future action that will change our bodies and conform them to his. 3. In Romans 8:29, God has "predestined [his children] to be conformed to the image of his Son": here, the resemblance is spiritual and moral, an inner conformity to the character of Christ. It is not a mere outward imitation, but a true transformation of our nature.
G4832.origine: The word comes from the prefix "σύν" (syn, together) and "μορφή" (morphè, form). It literally means "having the same form." This vocabulary of form refers to the "morphè" of Christ — his divine radiance and glory — and that of God the Father. To be similar to Christ is to share in his glorified form, first in the moral and spiritual order here below, and then in the physical order at the resurrection.
G4832.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times by Paul, and both to speak of our resemblance to Christ. In Romans 8:29, it describes the ultimate purpose of divine election: God chose us to be conformed to Christ, to share in his life. In Philippians 3:21, it is Christ himself who will act to make us similar to him by resurrecting our bodies and transforming them into glorious bodies. These two passages complete the process: God predestines us for this conformity, and Christ will accomplish it by his power.
G4832.portee: This word conveys an extraordinary promise to the believer. We are not destined to remain as we are; we are called to a progressive transformation, first moral and spiritual in this life, then physical and definitive at the resurrection. This establishes the assurance that our life in Christ has a purpose: to become like him, to share in his glory, to reflect his character. It is both a call to present sanctification and a glorious hope for the future.

sens: To become similar to someone in form, appearance, or condition
To be transformed into the image of someone by participating in their experience
To identify with someone by sharing what they are going through
G4833.detail:
1. The word literally evokes the act of taking on the same form as someone else. In Philippians 3:10, Paul speaks of becoming conformed to Christ in his death: this is not merely about outward resemblance, but about sharing inwardly the same condition, the same experience.
2. It is a deeper transformation than simple imitation: Paul desires to be shaped into the image of Christ by sharing in the fellowship of his sufferings. This conformity occurs progressively, through the action of the Spirit and participation in the life of Christ.
3. The verse shows that this conformity is not an end in itself, but a means to better know Christ and attain resurrection. It is a dynamic union with Christ in his death and life.
G4833.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "syn" (with) and "morphe" (form, appearance). The basic image is that of transformation, of conforming in form. It is a passive verb: one is transformed, one becomes conformed, rather than transforming oneself. This root "morphe" is found in other biblical words expressing transformation and resemblance.
G4833.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 3:10. Paul uses it to express his deep desire to become conformed to Christ, particularly by sharing in his sufferings and death. It is an expression of the disciple's journey: following Christ is not merely believing in him or imitating him from afar, but progressively being transformed into his image. This passage is at the heart of Paul's theology of identification with Christ in his passion.
G4833.portee: This word calls the believer to a deep transformation, not just moral or behavioral, but an intimate union with Christ. To become conformed to him means accepting to share not only in his future glory but also in his present sufferings. It is an invitation to go beyond superficial imitation to enter into a real participation in the life of Christ and his sacrificial love.

sens: To share the feelings or sufferings of someone
To feel compassion for the difficulties of others
To identify with the condition or pain of another
G4834.detail:
1. To sympathize literally means "to suffer with": it is to actively share the feelings, pains, or weaknesses of someone else. The word expresses a participation of heart and mind in what another experiences. In Hebrews 4:15, we learn that Jesus sympathizes with our weaknesses: he is not distant or indifferent to our struggles, but understands them from within because he himself has been tempted.
2. To sympathize can also refer to the action of showing compassion to someone in need or suffering. In Hebrews 10:34, the early Christians had compassion for the prisoners: they felt their pain and acted to help them, even accepting the loss of their own possessions.
3. The word expresses an emotional and moral communion with the one who suffers, a form of active empathy where one does not merely pity but truly enters into the condition of the other.
G4834.origine: The Greek word συμπαθέω is formed from the prefix σύν (sun: "with") and πάθος (pathos: "suffering, feeling, passion"). It literally designates the act of "suffering or feeling with". This family of words always evokes an inner participation in the emotions or pains of others. The composition of the word emphasizes the emotional bond and solidarity: one does not sympathize from afar, but by uniting with the one who suffers.
G4834.emploi: The verb to sympathize appears twice in the New Testament, both times in Hebrews, and in both cases it describes a profound reality of the relationship between Jesus and his disciples, or among Christians themselves. In Hebrews 4:15, it qualifies the ability of the Great High Priest Jesus to understand and share human weaknesses. In Hebrews 10:34, it describes the emotional and practical response of believers toward those who suffer for their faith. These two uses show that to sympathize is not a mere passive feeling, but a posture of commitment and solidarity: Jesus sympathizes by interceding for us, Christians sympathize by helping the persecuted.
G4834.portee: This word reminds the Christian that Jesus is not a distant and insensitive God, but that he entered into the human condition and truly understands our struggles and pains. It also invites the believer to imitate this compassion toward those who suffer, not out of formal duty, but through a genuine union of heart. To sympathize calls for both trust — our Great High Priest understands us — and action — we must sympathize with others as Christ has sympathized with us.

sens: Who feels the same feelings as another
Who is capable of sharing the feelings and pains of others
G4835.detail:
1. This word describes someone who feels the same emotions, the same thoughts as another person. It is to be in deep harmony with someone else. In 1 Peter 3:8, Peter exhorts believers to be "of one mind and one spirit": having this shared feeling creates unity in the community.
2. Beyond mere identity of thought, the word also suggests the ability to sympathize, to suffer with others. One who is "of the same sentiment" does not remain indifferent to the pains of their neighbor; they enter into what they feel. It is a form of active compassion, rooted in a common sensitivity.
G4835.origine: The word is formed from two elements: *syn-* ("with", "together") and *pathēs* (derived from *pathein*, "to suffer", "to experience"). It belongs to the family of Greek words expressing passion and suffering. The basic image is that of shared suffering or emotion, felt together. That is why the word encompasses both the idea of a common thought and that of sincere compassion.
G4835.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 3:8. Peter uses it to exhort the church to inner unity: believers should not only think alike on paper, but *feel together*, in their hearts, the same feelings of compassion, brotherly love, and humility. It is a call to a harmony that is truly internal and emotional, not just intellectual or superficial.
G4835.portee: This word reminds the Christian that unity in the church is not primarily a matter of organization, but of shared heart. To be "of the same sentiment" means to allow oneself to be transformed to enter into what the other feels, to weep with those who weep, to rejoice with those who rejoice. It is an invitation to mutual vulnerability and active compassion, lasting foundations of authentic brotherhood.

sens: To stand close to someone to support or help them
To be present together at a show or event
G4836.detail:
1. The verb primarily expresses the idea of coming alongside someone, presenting oneself to help or defend them. It is an act of solidarity or support.
2. It can also simply mean to be there, in a crowd, to attend an event, like the spectators watching a performance (Luke 23:48: the crowd attending the crucifixion of Christ).
G4836.origine: The word is composed of three Greek elements: "syn" (together), "para" (beside), and "ginomai" (to come, to appear). This composition creates the image of coming together alongside someone. In ancient Greek, this verb is found in historians like Thucydides to describe the action of gathering or coming to aid. The root "ginomai" is very common in Greek and always carries the idea of becoming or presence.
G4836.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 23:48. It describes the crowd that attends the crucifixion of Christ: all those who were gathered to watch this spectacle are present together at this decisive moment. The context shows that the verb here means to be there as a spectator of a major event, without necessarily providing active help, but simply sharing presence at that moment.
G4836.portee: This word reminds us that the crucifixion of Christ was not a hidden event: a crowd was there, witnessing his death. For the Christian, this raises a question: are we truly present at the decisive moments of our faith, or just passing by? To be truly present means being able to let the event transform us, like the crowd that ultimately struck their chests in recognition of what had happened.

sens: To call someone to act with strength and authority, in the company of others
To strengthen someone morally or spiritually with comforting words
To mutually support each other's courage and confidence in a shared trial or faith
G4837.detail:
1. The verb combines the idea of calling to action ("kaléô") with that of accompaniment ("syn" = together). It involves exhorting someone with strength, not alone but in a group, as one encourages a friend to join in a common effort.

2. In Paul's spiritual context, this word means "to strengthen" or "to comfort" — not with soft words, but with vigorous exhortation that revives moral energy. It is the force of "parakaléô" (to console by encouraging) amplified by "sun" (together).

3. In Romans 1:12, Paul tells the Christians in Rome that he desires to be "encouraged together" with them by their mutual faith: it is a reciprocal support, where each revives the strength of the other in a communion of trust. The image is that of warriors encouraging each other before battle.
G4837.origine: The word is composed of three elements: "syn" (together), "para" (beside, with), and "kaléô" (to call). This composition doubles the idea of exhortation by adding the communal aspect. The simple word "parakaléô" (to comfort, to exhort) appears more than a hundred times in the New Testament, especially in Paul; the prefix "syn" reinforces the mutual and collective aspect. It is a living word from the Pauline epistles to describe church life.
G4837.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Romans 1:12. Paul uses it to express his desire to meet the Christians in Rome: he wants not only to exhort them but to be exhorted by them in return. It is a rare and chosen verb, emphasizing the reciprocity of spiritual encouragement. Paul rejects the idea of a one-way relationship (the teacher teaching the passive disciple); he hopes that their shared faith will be a source of mutual edification. The context shows that this encouragement together is rooted in "the faith that we share," a shared trust in Jesus Christ.
G4837.portee: This word reminds Christians that faith is not a solitary affair. Spiritual encouragement is given and received within the community of the church. No one is too mature to be strengthened by another's faith; no one is too weak to strengthen their brother. This reciprocity destroys pride and passivity, making Christian life a living mutual aid.

sens: To take someone or something to accompany in a movement
To associate someone with a mission or undertaking
G4838.detail:
1. To take someone with you when leaving a place, so that they physically accompany you. The idea is to seize and lead together. Barnabas and Saul, after completing their mission in Jerusalem, "take" John Mark with them (Acts 12:25), and Barnabas wants to "take" John Mark for a new journey (Acts 15:37).
2. To deliberately bring someone to participate in an action, mission, or project. Paul "takes" Titus with him when he goes up to Jerusalem (Galatians 2:1), designating him as a companion in his undertaking; conversely, Paul refuses to "take" John Mark because he had previously abandoned the team (Acts 15:38).
G4838.origine: The Greek word is formed from three elements: "syn" (with), "para" (beside, together), and "lambanô" (to take, to seize). This composition creates the image of taking something or someone "with you" to lead them. In Hebrew, the corresponding verb is often "saphah" (to clasp, to draw together) or "shalach" (to send, to lead). The basic meaning is always that of a common action where one takes or leads a companion.
G4838.emploi: This verb appears four times in the New Testament, exclusively in Luke's writings in Acts and in Paul in Galatians. The three occurrences in Acts recount the debate between Barnabas and Paul regarding John Mark's fate: Barnabas wants to "take" him again (15:37), but Paul refused to "take" him with them (15:38) after he had abandoned them. Galatians 2:1 shows Paul "taking" Titus with him. The usage thus reveals the idea of a *deliberate selection*: the one taken along is an accepted companion for the task, and the one refused is excluded. The verb marks less the simple transport than the *missionary choice*.
G4838.portee: This word speaks to us about the communion of Christian service. Taking someone along is not a logistical detail: it is recognizing their dedication and integrating them into one's mission. The refusal to take John Mark (who had deserted) shows that faithfulness matters. For today's Christian, this verb reminds us that those who accompany us in service must be trustworthy partners and that our obedience to God sometimes requires difficult relational choices.

sens: To be there together with someone, to share their presence
G4840.detail: 1. The word literally means to be together and to be present at the same time. It is a verb that combines the idea of companionship ("with") and physical presence. In Acts 25:24, Festus speaks to the notable figures who are "present with" him in the court to judge the apostle Paul — they are there in the same room, at the same time, all gathered for this official hearing.
G4840.origine: The word is composed of the prefix συν (sun) meaning "with, together" and the verb πάρειμι (pareimi) meaning "to be present, to be there." This composition emphasizes the idea of shared presence, of co-presence. The simple verb πάρειμι often appears in Greek to denote mere physical presence.
G4840.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 25:24. Paul stands before the Roman governor Festus and King Agrippa; Festus emphasizes that all the important dignitaries are present with him for this hearing. The context is that of an official assembly, a court of justice where the presence of multiple witnesses and personalities invests the trial with public solemnity. The word emphasizes not only the fact of being there but also the fact of being together, being present collectively.
G4840.portee: This word reminds us of the value of presence — not only that of God but that of others with us in important moments. When the Gospel is at stake and faith must be defended or witnessed, the presence of brothers and witnesses matters. This also speaks to those who must face a trial: knowing that others are "present with" them in their struggle is a form of support and encouragement.

sens: Endure the same pain as another person or with them
Share someone else's suffering out of sympathy
Experience compassion through suffering
G4841.detail:
1. Suffering together means going through the same trials: in Romans 8:17, Paul says that if we are children of God, we must suffer with Christ, meaning sharing in His afflictions and tribulations before sharing in His glory. It is an active and voluntary participation in the sufferings of Christ.
2. In the body of the Church, suffering with means that when one member endures pain, all the other members feel it too: in 1 Corinthians 12:26, if one member suffers, all the members suffer together with him, because they form one body. The suffering of one becomes the suffering of all.
3. Suffering with also expresses compassion: it is to unite with the pain of others, not to remain an indifferent spectator, but to truly enter into their trial and share it from the heart.
G4841.origine: The word is composed of two elements: "sun" (σύν) meaning "with, together," and "paschô" (πάσχω) meaning "to suffer, to endure." The image is one of shared pain, where several people endure together. The verb "paschô" primarily evokes physical or moral suffering, but also passion (the word "passion" comes from the same root). In classical Greek, this compound verb can also express emotional sympathy towards the one who suffers.
G4841.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In Romans 8:17, Paul uses it to urge believers to accept suffering with Christ as a condition for eternal glorification: it is a Christological suffering, linked to our union with the Lord. In 1 Corinthians 12:26, he describes the functioning of the body of the Church: the suffering of one member affects the whole body, expressing the interdependence of Christians. In both cases, it is shared suffering, not isolated: it creates a bond, either with Christ or among brothers and sisters.
G4841.portee: This word reminds Christians that faith does not exempt them from suffering, but invites them to go through it with Christ and with one another. Suffering with Christ means entering into His death to rise with Him; suffering with the Church means cultivating true fraternal solidarity where no one suffers alone. This verse frees from the illusion of a Christian life without trials and directs towards the hope of common glorification.

sens: Send someone accompanied by another person
Dispatch together, as a coordinated group
G4842.detail:
1. Sending someone by having them accompanied by another person: this is a sending that is not solitary, but creates unity with a third party. In 2 Corinthians 8:18, Paul says, "we are sending with him the brother whose praise regarding the Gospel is well known" — the brother travels not alone, but in the company of the one just mentioned.
2. More broadly, dispatching together, as a delegation or a team: the word emphasizes that several go together for the same mission. In 2 Corinthians 8:22, Paul adds, "we are sending with them our brother" — again, this is not an isolated sending, but a coordinated sending, where the brother joins the group going to the place.
G4842.origine: The word is composed of the prefix σύν (syn-, "with") and the verb πέμπω (pempō, "to send"). This composition creates a verb that expresses not just sending, but sending together, in company. The prefix syn- is very productive in Greek for forming verbs that indicate union or collaboration: syn-ergos (one who works with), syn-éreia (collaboration), etc.
G4842.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in 2 Corinthians 8, in the same section where Paul organizes a collection for the church in Jerusalem. He speaks of sending brothers as reliable delegates and messengers who will carry the gifts. The context is one of trust and responsibility: Paul carefully chooses who to send with whom, so that the transport of these donations is honorable and blameless. The verb marks the importance of the bond between the sent ones and the unity of their mission.
G4842.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that responsibilities and missions are not borne alone, but in the company of trustworthy brothers. It is a call to solidarity and the coordinated sending of believers: one does not entrust an important work to an isolated person, but to a group where agreement and mutual trust prevail. This also emphasizes the importance of carefully choosing the messengers of the Church and sending them together for testimony and credibility.

sens: surround someone with one's arms
embrace, hold close
G4843.detail:
1. The verb literally means to surround or enclose something or someone with one's arms, putting them around the person or object. It is the image of a concrete gesture: Paul bends down to the young Eutychus who fell from the third story and "takes him in his arms" to reassure him and perhaps warm him (Acts 20:10).
2. Figuratively, it is also a gesture of affection, welcome, or comfort, where the arms embrace the one we love or wish to console.
G4843.origine: The word is composed of three elements: "syn" (with, together), "peri" (around), and "lambano" (to take, to seize). The basic idea is therefore "to take someone around," that is, to surround them with one's arms. This composition clearly shows the image of the gesture: one surrounds the person by seizing them.
G4843.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 20:10, where Paul, after the fall of the young Eutychus, bends down to him and takes him in his arms. It is a moment of tenderness and pastoral compassion: Paul reacts with a gesture of human and warm contact to reassure the disciples and show that the young man is well. The context reveals a Paul attentive to the physical and emotional well-being of those he loves.
G4843.portee: This verse shows that the Christian faith is not abstract: it is also expressed through contact, embrace, and physical presence. Paul's example reminds the reader that to console someone is also to know how to touch and surround them, not just to speak to them. In our fraternal relationships, this gesture of embrace expresses the concrete love and mutual support that Christ calls His Church to live out.

sens: Share a meal or drink with someone
Eat and drink together as a sign of communion
Participate in a common feast or banquet
G4844.detail:
1. The verb literally means to drink together, in the company of another person. It is a simple and concrete action: when one drinks with someone, they are at the table beside them, sharing the same moment and the same table.
2. This expression evokes much more than the mere act of drinking: it implies communion, brotherhood, shared intimacy. Eating and drinking together in the ancient world was an act loaded with social and spiritual significance, marking an alliance or mutual acceptance (Acts 10:41).
3. The context of Acts 10:41 shows that the apostles who "ate and drank with" the resurrected Jesus were chosen as privileged witnesses of his resurrection. This common consumption was not a mere snack, but the living proof that it was indeed a physical resurrection and not a spiritual vision.
G4844.origine: The word comes from the prefix "syn" (with) added to the verb "pinô" (to drink). This composition clearly shows that the meaning lies not only in the act of drinking, but in doing it together, which emphasizes the importance of communion rather than mere consumption.
G4844.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 10:41. Peter uses it to emphasize that the apostles are not merely eyewitnesses of the resurrection of Jesus, but intimate witnesses who shared a meal with him after he was resurrected. This detail is crucial: it shows that the resurrected Jesus had a real body, capable of eating and drinking, and was not a mere ghostly apparition.
G4844.portee: This word reminds the Christian that faith in the resurrected Christ does not rest on abstract theories, but on tangible testimonies. The apostles ate with him, they touched him, they shared his table: their faith was not naivety, but direct knowledge. For today's believer, this invites recognition that the resurrection is a historical event that marked the body and person of Jesus, and that those who followed him first had this conviction of being eyewitnesses.

sens: to fill with water to the brim (of a boat)
to be fulfilled, to reach its term (of time)
to complete, to carry out a process
G4845.detail:
1. The primary meaning is concrete: a boat that fills with water, submerged by the waves. In Luke 8:23, during the storm on the lake, the boat "fills with water" — a dramatic image of the danger threatening the disciples. The word evokes a complete filling, to the brim, which threatens to sink the ship.

2. The meaning extends to time that flows and is fulfilled: when "the time when Jesus was to be taken from the world approached," this time was "fulfilled," it reached its intended term (Luke 9:51). Similarly, at Pentecost, the day was completed, brought to its fulfillment (Acts 2:1). It is the idea that the time that was to come has come, that the promise has materialized.

3. More broadly, the verb expresses the fulfillment of a destiny, a project, or a deadline — bringing something to its intended conclusion, completing it fully.
G4845.origine: The word is formed from the prefix "syn-" (with, together) and "plèroô" (to fill). This composition reinforces the idea: not only to fill, but to fill completely, to the end. In Hebrew, the verb often translated is "mâlé" (to fill), but also "nâphal" (to fall) when it concerns an accomplishment that falls upon someone — the image of time that "falls" at its hour.
G4845.emploi: The verb appears only 3 times in the New Testament. In Luke 8:23, it literally describes the water flooding the boat during the storm — an immediate danger. In Luke 9:51 and Acts 2:1, it has a temporal or eschatological sense: the moment set by God arrives, is filled, is fulfilled. In these last two cases, it expresses the fulfillment of a divine word, of an established plan. The context is always that of a divine intervention or a crucial moment.
G4845.portee: This verb invites the reader to meditate on the fulfillment of God's promises. When time flows, it is never by chance: it "fills" according to God's plan. For Jesus, each step — his ascension, Pentecost — is fulfilled according to a traced destiny. This encourages the believer to trust God in storms and delays, knowing that God masters the times and brings his plans to fruition.

sens: To compress, squeeze tightly to the point of preventing breathing or growth
To be surrounded, pressed by a crowd that squeezes from all sides
To prevent a teaching or spiritual seed from producing its fruit
G4846.detail:
1. In the literal sense, the word describes physical asphyxiation: something tight blocks air or life. In Luke 8:42, Jesus is "pressed" by the crowd that pushes against him from all sides, compressing him in his walk.
2. Applied to a seed or plant, the word evokes thorns that grow around it, choking and suffocating it. In Mark 4:7, the seed falls among thorns that "choke" it by taking away space and resources for growth.
3. In a figurative and spiritual sense, the word designates anything that compresses and paralyzes the Word in the believer's heart. In Matthew 13:22 and Mark 4:19, it is the worries of the world, the desire for riches, and other cravings that "choke" the received Word, preventing it from producing spiritual fruit in life.
G4846.origine: The Greek word συμπνίγω is composed of συν- (with, together) and πνίγω (to choke, to squeeze). This composition reinforces the idea: it is not a simple squeezing, but a compression from all sides, as if multiple forces converge to suffocate. The root πνίγω itself evokes asphyxiation and death. The corresponding Hebrew word from the Old Testament would be from the family of חנק (to strangle).
G4846.emploi: The word appears five times in the Gospels, always with the idea of compression that blocks life. Once in the literal sense: in Luke 8:42, the crowd "presses" Jesus physically by squeezing him. Four times in the figurative sense, in the parable of the sower: in Mark 4:7 and 4:19, in Matthew 13:22 and in Luke 8:14, the thorns or the worries of the world "choke" the Word, that is to say, they prevent it from growing and bearing fruit in the heart. This passage from the physical image (crowd pressing) to the botanical image (thorns choking) then to the spiritual image (worldly concerns paralyzing faith) shows how Jesus uses the same word for all obstacles that hinder life.
G4846.portee: This word invites the believer to examine their heart: what is "choking" the Word within them? Not just raw unbelief, but daily distractions, material concerns, pleasures that gradually compress and paralyze their spiritual growth. It is a call not to let the thorns of this world choke the divine seed: vigilance and constant weeding of the heart are necessary for the Word to bear fruit.

sens: a person who shares the same citizenship, the same civic status
in a spiritual sense: a member of the same faith community, of the same people of God
G4847.detail:
1. The word primarily designates someone who enjoys the same citizenship, who belongs to the same city or state. It is a companion in civic and political life.
2. Paul uses it spiritually in Ephesians 2:19 to say that believers, who were once strangers to the covenant of Israel, have now become fellow citizens with the saints — that is, full members of the people of God, with all the rights and dignity that entails. The image of citizenship evokes equality of status and belonging to the same body.
G4847.origine: The word is composed of *syn* ("with") and *politês* ("citizen"), from *polis* ("city"). It literally evokes one who shares the same *polis*, the same organized community. It is a classical Greek word, well attested in ancient literature, that designates the civic solidarity of the inhabitants of the same city.
G4847.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Ephesians 2:19. Paul uses it to express the integration of converted Gentiles into the community of the people of God. He calls them "fellow citizens with the saints" to show that they are no longer strangers or temporary guests, but that they now enjoy equal belonging to the Church. The image of citizenship emphasizes that this integration is complete and irrevocable.
G4847.portee: This word encourages the believer to understand their entry into Christ as a true change of status: moving from exclusion to belonging, from strangeness to brotherly equality. It is a promise of dignity and stability within the people of God, based not on human merits but on grace.

sens: To journey together, to travel in company
To gather, to assemble around someone
G4848.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of traveling or walking together: several people are walking along a path in the same direction, side by side. It is the image of a company accompanying someone. In Luke 7:11, the disciples and a large crowd are walking with Jesus as he goes to Nain; in Luke 24:15, Jesus himself walks with two disciples on the road to Emmaus without them initially recognizing him.
2. A second meaning is that of gathering or assembling around someone: the crowd gathers and focuses around a person to listen to or follow them. In Mark 10:1, after Jesus departs, the crowd gathers again near him, and he teaches them. This meaning emphasizes less the movement than the convergence towards a common point or person.
G4848.origine: The word is formed from two elements: the prefix "syn-" ("with", "together") and "poreuomai" ("to walk", "to go", "to journey"). The basic image is that of common walking, of a shared path. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the Greek word often translates the verb "halak" which also means "to walk" or "to go". This composition reveals the idea of accompaniment and solidarity of the group in motion.
G4848.emploi: The verb appears four times in the Gospels, only in Luke and Mark. Luke uses it three times to describe groups walking with Jesus: first a large crowd with his disciples (7:11), then large crowds accompanying him (14:25), and finally Jesus himself walking with two resurrected disciples (24:15). Mark uses it once (10:1) to depict the crowd gathering around Jesus. The context varies, but the word always emphasizes physical accompaniment and common presence: it is never a mere distant following, but a true company.
G4848.portee: This word reminds the reader that following Jesus is never a solitary affair: it is a path shared with others. Whether walking with him like the crowd from Nain, being his disciples, or discovering his presence beside oneself as in Emmaus, there is always proximity, a true presence. This also speaks to the Christian life: we do not walk alone, but in a community, and Jesus himself accompanies us on the journey.

sens: A gathering of people sitting together to share a meal
An organized assembly of people seated at the same table or in the same place
G4849.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a gathering where people come together to eat and drink, particularly a banquet or a convivial meal. In Mark 6:39, Jesus orders the crowd to sit "in groups" on the green grass: each group forms a unit of diners seated together for the meal of the five thousand.
2. More broadly, it is an organized arrangement of people in small groups, each occupying a defined place. The image is that of an orderly assembly, where everyone has their place within a small collective.
G4849.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that evokes the idea of drinking together and gathering around a table. The term was borrowed from classical Greek where it designated the philosophical banquets (symposia) of Greek cities, notably in Athens. It expresses the idea of an assembly structured around a shared meal.
G4849.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 6:39. Jesus organizes the disciples and the crowd into "groups" seated on the grass before distributing the loaves and fish. This arrangement into groups makes possible both the counting of the diners and the orderly distribution of food. It is a practical detail that emphasizes how Jesus organizes even simple gestures with method and wisdom.
G4849.portee: This word shows us that organization and order are not foreign to spiritual life and miracles. Jesus does not feed the crowd chaotically, but arranges them into structured groups. This teaches the believer that God loves order and that even great divine works are accomplished according to a wisdom that organizes and sets in place.

sens: An elder of the Church who shares this role with others
A member of the leadership group of the local Church
G4850.detail: 1. The word designates an elder — that is, a leader or overseer of the Church — who exercises this role alongside other elders. Peter addresses the "elders" in 1 Peter 5:1, presenting himself as an "elder" on the same level as them: he does not speak from above, but as an equal, since he shares the same pastoral responsibility with them. 2. It is a term that emphasizes the idea of communion and solidarity in ministry: the elders are not isolated, but form a college or group of leaders who work together for the good of the Church.
G4850.origine: The word is formed from the prefix "with" (syn-) and the term "elder" (presbytéros) which literally means "older". In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the "elders" (zékénim) were the mature and experienced men who led the people. The prefix "with" adds the idea that this responsibility of elder is shared — it is not a solitary title, but a ministry exercised in community.
G4850.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 5:1. Peter uses it to address the elders of the local Church with great humility: while he was one of the leading apostles, he presents himself as their "fellow elder" rather than as their superior. This shows how, even in the early days of the Church, leadership was conceived as a ministry shared among several responsible individuals, and not as a solitary power or strict hierarchy.
G4850.portee: This word reminds the Christian that those who lead the Church act in solidarity, without claiming isolated authority. For the elders or leaders, it is a call to humility and unity: they are not masters who command alone, but brothers who share the same pastoral responsibility. For the entire Church, it is an assurance that Christian leadership is conceived as a communal and collegial ministry.

sens: to gather together, assemble
to be useful or profitable for someone
to be suitable for someone, to serve someone's interest
G4851.detail:
1. The primary meaning is concrete: to gather or assemble several things together. This is seen in Acts 19:19, where the books of magic are gathered into a pile to be burned.

2. The common meaning is to be useful or profitable. When John says, "it is advantageous that one man die for the people" (John 11:50), he means that this death will serve the collective interest — it is more advantageous, more beneficial for all. Paul also uses it: "it is not useful" to say in public (1 Corinthians 6:12).

3. Often the word expresses suitability or opportunity: what best serves our interests or those of others. In Matthew 5:29, Jesus says it is "advantageous" to deprive oneself of a member rather than to be thrown entirely into hell — it is the choice that truly serves our good, even if it costs.
G4851.origine: The word is composed of two parts: "sum" (with, together) and "phérô" (to bear, to bring). The basic image is that of bearing together, gathering. From there comes the meaning of putting together for the benefit of someone — what brings together advantages, what profits. The root "phérô" is found in many Greek words of the New Testament related to the idea of bearing or producing.
G4851.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul and in the Gospels. Almost always it is the impersonal form "it is advantageous" (συμφέρει) that prevails: it emphasizes the objective advantage, what truly suits, regardless of personal desires. Jesus uses it several times to state a hard truth — that it is better to lose an eye than to be damned (Matthew 5:29-30), or that it is wiser for one innocent man to die to save the nation (John 11:50 and 18:14). Paul uses it to discern Christian freedom: everything is permissible, but not everything is advantageous (1 Corinthians 6:12, 10:23). Also in the neutral sense: what is useful, beneficial, like the teaching Paul gives publicly (Acts 20:20).
G4851.portee: This word invites the Christian to go beyond momentary preferences to seek true good — for oneself and for others. Jesus uses it to justify sacrifices that seem unjust or unpleasant: losing a member rather than sinning (Matthew 5:29), dying for the nation (John 11:50). It is a call to see beyond the immediate. Paul uses it to balance freedom in Christ: we have the right to do many things, but true wisdom requires choosing what truly benefits — oneself and the community of believers.

sens: To give one's agreement, consent to something
To confess, openly admit something
G4852.detail:
1. To recognize here means to give one's agreement to a statement, to consent to it. In Romans 7:16, Paul says that by doing wrong against his will, he "recognizes" or "confesses" through his actions that God's law is good: his involuntary behavior testifies to the excellence of the divine law, even though his flesh transgresses it.
2. The word can also mean to admit, to openly confess: it is to acknowledge a truth, to express agreement with it, to declare it publicly or in the judgment of one's own conscience.
G4852.origine: The Greek word σύμφημι is composed of the prefix σύν ("with", "together") and the verb φημι ("to say", "to speak"). The starting image is therefore "to say together with", that is, to speak with one voice, hence "to agree with", "to consent to". This root φημι is found in other biblical words related to speech and affirmation.
G4852.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 7:16. Paul uses it to describe how our involuntary behavior confesses or recognizes the excellence of God's law. Even when we fail to keep it, our failures themselves attest that this law is just and good, because we desire it inwardly. This word expresses the inner assent that manifests in our actions, despite the weakness of our flesh.
G4852.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize that God's law is good, even in the face of his own failure. It reveals a deep paradox: it is precisely in failing that we confess the beauty of the divine law. This encourages us not to despair of our weaknesses, but to see them as proof that our heart truly longs for good, and to turn to God's grace in Christ to find the strength we lack.

sens: A person of the same people, of the same nation
A member of the same community or tribe of origin
G4853.detail:
1. This word literally designates someone who shares the same tribe or people as oneself. In 1 Thessalonians 2:14, Paul uses it to speak of the Thessalonians who suffered "from your own compatriots": this refers to the inhabitants of Thessalonica who persecuted their Christian brothers simply because they lived in the same city and region.
2. The meaning broadens to any person sharing the same nation or community of origin. Paul draws a parallel between the sufferings of the Thessalonians and those of the churches in Judea, showing that Christians everywhere face opposition from their own fellow citizens.
G4853.origine: The Greek word is composed of two elements: σύν (syn, "with") and φυλή (phylē, "tribe"). This root phylē refers to the idea of tribe, people, a group constitutive of a nation. The whole word thus literally means "one who shares the same tribe". It is a term formed to express solidarity of origin.
G4853.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Thessalonians 2:14. Paul uses it to refer to the inhabitants of Thessalonica who persecuted the new Christians from their own city. By using this term, the apostle highlights the painful irony: it is not strangers who oppose the Christians, but the members of their own community, their compatriots. This makes the persecution more personal and harder to bear.
G4853.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that opposition to faith can come from those closest to us — from those we thought shared the same heritage or identity. It is a word of compassion for all those who are rejected by their own people because of their commitment to Christ. It invites us to seek our true identity not in a nation or earthly tribe, but in the global community of believers.

sens: That has grown together with something, forming a single plant
That is connected to something in a way as natural and inseparable as intertwined roots
That shares the fate or condition of someone in an intimate and supportive manner
G4854.detail:
1. The word first evokes a concrete image: two plants or two stems that have grown together from the ground, their roots and stems forming a single organism. In Romans 6:5, Paul uses this image to describe Christians who have become "one plant with him [Christ] by conformity to his death."
2. In a broader sense, "growth united" describes a bond as natural and deep as that of common growth: what has grown together cannot be separated without harm. It is an organic bond, not a mere external attachment.
3. Spiritually, Paul uses it to express that we are united with Christ in his death and resurrection—our destiny is linked to his as the roots of a plant are united to the soil.
G4854.origine: The word comes from σύν ("with") and φύω ("to grow, to produce"). The image is that of joint growth: two things that have grown together. It is a rare word in classical Greek, but Paul chooses it to express the most intimate and organic union between Christians and Christ.
G4854.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 6:5. Paul uses it to explain baptism and our participation in the death and resurrection of Christ. He literally says that we have "become one plant with him"—that is, we have grown together with Christ to the point of sharing his fate. This botanical image emphasizes that union with Christ is not a superficial bond, but as deep and natural as growth itself.
G4854.portee: This image of common growth speaks to the Christian of their real union with Christ: it is not merely a mental decision or an external affiliation, but a belonging as deep and natural as that of a branch to a trunk or a root to soil. It invites us to understand that our death to sin and our resurrection to new life in Christ are not isolated acts, but realities that bind us to him inseparably.

sens: To grow at the same time as something else
To grow in contact with, to intertwine with
To develop jointly
G4855.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical and concrete: it is the fact that two plants or two elements grow together, in the same place, intertwined. In the parable of the sower in Luke 8:7, the thorns grow with the seed that has fallen among them, and this simultaneous growth means they intertwine and choke it.

2. The word can also express the idea of growth that occurs in close, even fusion-like contact: not only do the two elements grow at the same time, but they become inseparable, each affecting the growth of the other. The thorns and the grain do not just exist side by side; they grow together, entwined, and one destroys the chances of the other.
G4855.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "syn-" (with, together) and the verb "phuō" (to grow, to produce), which evokes the image of nature growing, of plant life developing. The root "phuō" is common in Greek to describe the natural growth of plants and living beings. This composition "together + grow" literally paints the idea of two things developing side by side.
G4855.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Luke 8:7, in the parable of the sower. Jesus uses it to describe how the thorns "grew" with the seed that fell among them. It is a word chosen to emphasize not only the concurrent presence of the two elements but the intimacy of their mutual growth and the effect of one on the other: the thorns do not just grow; they grow with the grain, making it impossible to harvest. The parabolic context gives the word a spiritual significance: it illustrates how the world, sin, and material concerns can grow with the Word sown in the heart and choke it.
G4855.portee: This word invites the reader to see that spiritual growth does not exist in a vacuum. Like the grain sown among thorns, faith encounters obstacles that grow with it: the worries of the world, wealth, pleasures. The Christian must recognize this inevitable struggle and ensure that their faith is free from what grows with it to choke it. It is a call to examination and vigilance.

sens: To be in agreement, to concur together
To agree on a price, a remuneration
To match, to correspond
To conspire together with a bad intention
G4856.detail:
1. To agree means to be in accord, to share the same will or conviction. When two people agree, they think and want the same thing: "If two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them" (Matthew 18:19). It is a harmony of heart and mind.

2. To agree on a price means to negotiate and reach a mutual understanding on an amount: the vineyard owner "agreed with them for a denarius a day" (Matthew 20:2). Both parties accept the same rate.

3. To match means that two elements fit together well, like "the piece he took is not matched to the old" garment (Luke 5:36). The image is one of natural harmony, a material harmony.

4. To agree together can also describe a guilty understanding, a conspiracy: Peter asks Sapphira, "How is it that you have agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord?" (Acts 5:9), revealing a pact in deceit.
G4856.origine: The word comes from the composition συμ- ("with") and φωνή ("voice, sound"). The starting image is that of voices harmonizing, sounding well together—hence the proper sense of musical agreement. The metaphor has extended to any agreement, any mutual understanding. That is why in Greek this verb literally means "to sound together."
G4856.emploi: The verb appears 6 times in the New Testament. Matthew uses it twice to talk about negotiating a price (20:2, 20:13): it is a very concrete sense. Matthew and Luke also use it for agreement in prayer or the harmony of biblical texts (Matthew 18:19, Luke 5:36, Acts 15:15). In particular, in Acts 5:9, Luke gives the verb a severe moral nuance: to agree becomes to conspire, to collude to deceive. Everywhere, the meaning is that of a meeting of two wills or two elements that coincide.
G4856.portee: This word reminds the believer of the power of unanimous agreement in prayer and common action. When two Christians sincerely agree according to God's will, God responds to their request. But the word also warns: an agreement can be a trap, a complicity in evil, as shown by the case of Ananias and Sapphira. It is therefore an invitation to seek harmony in truth and justice.

sens: Harmony, mutual understanding between two or more people
Common consent, agreement of mind and will
G4857.detail:
1. The word describes harmony, a mutual understanding between two people or two groups who share the same thoughts, the same principles. It is the idea of a symphony where all the instruments play together in the same key. In 2 Corinthians 6:15, Paul uses it to pose a rhetorical question: can there be such harmony, such understanding between Christ and Belial, between the believer and the unbeliever?
2. More broadly, it is mutual consent, the agreement of will between partners. This agreement implies a community of faith, values, and direction. Without it, there can be no true, lasting, and fruitful association.
G4857.origine: The word comes from the root "syn" (with, together) and "phōnē" (voice, sound). Literally, it means "to sound together." It is from the same family as "symphony" and "telephone." The Greek word conveys the idea of a unanimous voice, of harmony where all partners speak with one voice and walk in the same direction.
G4857.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 6:15, in a passage where Paul warns believers against unequal associations with unbelievers. He uses this term to express the impossibility of true harmony, of a deep agreement between one who follows Christ and one who rejects His lordship. It is a strong term, emphasizing that the difference in faith creates a fundamental incompatibility, not just a superficial one.
G4857.portee: This word reminds Christians that a lasting association, especially in marriage or significant partnerships, requires harmony of faith and values. Without this agreement on essential issues — who Jesus is, how to live — the relationship will lack a solid foundation. It is a call to seek unity with those who share your conviction that Christ is Lord.

sens: The art of combining sounds to create a composition pleasing to the ear
A set of sounds produced by instruments or voices
Melodious and organized noise
G4858.detail: 1. Music is the art of assembling sounds in a harmonious and pleasant way: it arises from the organized combination of melodies and rhythms. This is the primary meaning of the Greek word, which comes from "symphony" (sound together). 2. In the Bible, the word concretely refers to the sounds produced by musical instruments or voices that sing. In Luke 15:25, when the elder son "heard the music and the dancing," it is the joyful and organized noise of a celebration where musicians play instruments to accompany the festivities. 3. More broadly, it refers to anything that resonates melodiously, creating a festive or solemn atmosphere. The word can also refer to the instrument itself (lyre, flute, harp) that produces these sounds.
G4858.origine: The Greek word comes from "symphonos" (συμφωνος), which literally means "sounding together," composed of "syn" (with) and "phônè" (sound). It evokes the idea of sounds that agree and harmonize. This root also appears in the French word "symphonie." In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, it is notably the Hebrew word "sumponiya" (סוּמְפּוֹנְיָה) borrowed from neighboring languages that is rendered by this term: it is a word for joyful and noisy music.
G4858.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Luke 15:25, in the parable of the prodigal son. It is precisely at the moment when the father celebrates the return of his younger son with a great joyful feast. The elder son, returning from the fields, hears "the music and the dancing" — that is, the festive music of a celebration. This context shows that music was an essential element of rejoicing and feasting in biblical culture.
G4858.portee: This word reminds us that joy and celebration have their place in the life of the believer. The scene in Luke 15 illustrates how music and festivity mark the father's love for his found son. For the reader, it is an invitation to recognize that God rejoices at the return of the one who was lost, and that heavenly joy is not austere, but festive and full of music.

sens: That sounds together, producing harmony
That agrees, that is in accord
By mutual agreement, by mutual consent
G4859.detail:
1. In the literal sense, the word describes sounds that harmonize together, like voices or instruments that sound right together. This is the basic image: "συν" (together) + "φωνή" (sound, voice).
2. In a figurative sense, it denotes the agreement between people who think alike, who are in harmony in their will. It is as if their hearts "sound" the same note.
3. In biblical practice, the expression "of their common agreement" (ἐκ συμφώνου) means that two or more people voluntarily agree, by mutual consent. In 1 Corinthians 7:5, Paul uses it to speak of spouses who abstain together from marital relations "by mutual agreement": it is their common will that guides this decision.
G4859.origine: The word comes from two Greek elements: "συν" (sun, together) and "φωνή" (phonè, sound, voice). The image is musical: like two instruments or two voices that sound in harmony. In Hebrew, this mutual agreement can be designated by terms that express union or conformity between wills.
G4859.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians 7:5. Paul uses it to address a delicate issue among the Corinthians: spouses may temporarily abstain from intimate relations, but only if both decide together, "by mutual agreement." The word emphasizes that this abstention must never be imposed by one on the other, but accepted by both. It is a unique case where grace is manifested through mutual agreement.
G4859.portee: This word reminds believers that Christian marriage is a shared commitment, where major decisions must be made together, in mutual respect. Agreement is not mere passive tolerance, but true heart consent. It is a protection against control or emotional manipulation within the couple.

sens: To calculate together the total amount of something
To evaluate the price or value of a set of objects
G4860.detail:
1. The verb literally means "to count together": it is to add numbers to make a total. In Acts 19:19, after the magicians of Ephesus burned their books of sorcery, they "estimate" their value together, that is, they calculate how much all those books were worth: fifty thousand pieces of silver.
2. More broadly, it is to evaluate or recognize the value of something. The calculation is not only mathematical: it is also a judgment on what something is truly worth.
G4860.origine: The word is formed from the prefix "syn-" ("together") and "psëphizô" ("to count, to calculate"), which itself comes from "psëphos" ("pebble, token"). The ancients counted with pebbles or tokens placed on an abacus, hence the image of calculation. It is a rare verb in biblical Greek: it appears only once in the New Testament.
G4860.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Acts 19:19. It is the moment when Paul preaches in Ephesus and the inhabitants, touched by the Gospel, renounce magic. The magicians burn their books and instruments, and the text says they "estimate" together their total value: fifty thousand pieces of silver (a huge sum for the time). The word emphasizes the extraordinary nature of this gesture: these men renounce a fortune to follow Jesus.
G4860.portee: This passage shows the transformative power of the Gospel: men who derived their wealth and power from occult practices completely renounce them. When they "estimate" the value of their burned books, they measure the price of inner change. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to reflect: what do I have in my life that I hold precious, but that the Gospel calls me to abandon?

sens: Sharing the same inner life, the same feelings
In deep agreement, in spirit and heart
G4861.detail:
1. The word paints the image of people who have one "soul" — that is, a shared inner life, the same dispositions of the heart. In Philippians 2:2, Paul urges Christians to be "of one soul," meaning to share not only ideas but a true communion of heart and spirit.
2. This means being in deep agreement, beyond words: thinking alike, loving alike, feeling alike. Unity is not superficial (a mere facade of agreement), but comes from a common inner transformation — all believers animated by the same Spirit, the same love of Christ.
G4861.origine: The word combines two elements: "syn-" (with, together) and "psuché" (soul, the inner life, the seat of feelings and will). It is a constructed word to express spiritual unity. The "soul" in Hebrew (nepesh) refers to the whole person in its vital and emotional dimension. The Greek word translates this notion of a common life, of inner communion.
G4861.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Philippians 2:2. Paul uses it to describe the unity that the Christians of Philippi must achieve — a unity of feeling and thought, beyond divisions or tensions. It is a word chosen to depict the deep harmony of those who live together in faith: not just tolerance, but true communion of spirit.
G4861.portee: This word reminds the reader that Christian unity is not a superficial command: it is a communion of the soul, a true sharing of the same convictions and the same love of Christ. It requires a transformation of the heart, not merely actions. For a church or community, it is an invitation not to settle for external peace, but to cultivate true spiritual harmony.

sens: in the company of, alongside
together, at the same time or in the same place
in a relationship of alliance, partisanship
equipped with, provided with
at the same time as, simultaneously with
G4862.detail:
1. The most common meaning is that of being present next to someone: being with him, going with him, walking together. John 21:3 gives a simple example: the disciples go fishing "with" Peter — they are there, together. Acts 14:28: the apostles "remained a long time with the disciples" — a prolonged presence, a shared life.
2. When several people or things are enumerated "with" others, the word expresses the idea of a parallel enumeration, almost like "and." Acts 25:23: Agrippa and Berenice enter "with" the tribunes, meaning in their company and on the same level. Luke 23:32: Jesus is crucified "with" two criminals — at the same time, in the same place.
3. The word can also express a relationship of alliance or partisanship. Acts 4:13: the authorities saw Peter and John who had been "with" Jesus — this communion reveals where their loyalty lay.
4. "With" can mean: equipped with, accompanied by. Matthew 25:27: the money returns "with" interest — it is increased by that interest.
5. The eternal dimension: "living with Jesus" (2 Corinthians 13:4) expresses the union of believers with Christ, not only in physical presence but in shared power and destiny.
G4862.origine: The preposition σύν comes from ancient Greek (Attic form ξύν). It expresses the fundamental idea of association, of sharing. In Hebrew, the closest equivalent is את (with) or פ (with-together). This preposition was very common in ancient Greek, but it gradually gave way to μετά (meta) during the evolution of Greek. That is why it is comparatively rare in the New Testament: it appears mainly in Luke and Paul, while Matthew and John use it very little.
G4862.emploi: The preposition σύν appears 126 times in the New Testament, which would make it a common preposition, but it is unevenly distributed. It is very frequent in Luke (in the Gospel and Acts) and in Paul, while Matthew and Mark use it rarely. It expresses very concrete realities (walking with someone, eating with someone, sitting with someone) as well as spiritual realities (living with Jesus, being with God). The examples show how the word adapts: sometimes it emphasizes simple physical presence (Luke 2:5, Joseph and Mary "with" the child), sometimes it implies true communion or alliance (Acts 4:13, the authorities recognize that the apostles have been "with" Jesus), and sometimes it brings two enumerations closer together (Acts 10:2, Cornelius prays to God "with" all his household).
G4862.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that faith does not isolate: it is lived in community, alongside other believers and — above all — alongside Christ. When Paul writes "we will live with him by the power of God" (2 Corinthians 13:4), this little preposition "with" expresses the intimacy of the believer's union with the risen Jesus. It also invites us to recognize Christ in those who have walked "with" him before us, and to cultivate the presence of one another as a spiritual good.

sens: To bring objects to one place, to collect them
To assemble people in the same location
To come together, to form a group
To welcome someone, to receive them
G4863.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to gather or collect material things: in John 6:13, they "gather" the leftover bread after the miracle of multiplication; in Luke 12:17-18, the rich man wonders where to "store up" his harvest. It is the idea of bringing scattered elements to one place.
2. Applied to people, it means to assemble or summon them: in Matthew 2:4, the king "gathered" the chief priests and scribes to inquire about the birthplace of the Messiah; the apostles "gather" around Jesus in Mark 6:30. The emphasis is on the intentional act of bringing people together.
3. The word can also describe the action of coming together spontaneously or forming a group: in Acts 11:26, the disciples "gathered" at the assemblies of the Church; in Matthew 22:34, the Pharisees "gathered" after a controversy. It is the communal dimension, the act of forming an assembly.
4. Finally, it carries the meaning of welcoming or receiving: in Matthew 25:35 and 38, having "gathered" the stranger means having received him hospitably, having given him hospitality — it is an act of kindness towards someone in distress.
G4863.origine: The word comes from the Greek prefix σύν (syn, "together") and the verb ἄγω (agō, "to lead, to conduct"). Literally, it means "to lead together." In Hebrew, it often translates אָסַף (asaf, "to gather, to assemble") and קָבַץ (qabats, "to assemble"), verbs evoking the regrouping of what is scattered. The Greek root ἄγω itself means to lead or guide, hence the sense of "leading together" to a common point.
G4863.emploi: The verb appears 61 times in the New Testament, especially in Matthew and in Acts. It is used to gather objects (harvest, food leftovers), but mainly to assemble people: religious authorities (Matthew 2:4, John 11:47), disciples (Mark 6:30), crowds (Mark 4:1), churches that gather to pray or teach (Acts 11:26, Acts 14:27). The passive "to be gathered" or "to gather" is very frequent: in Matthew 22:41 and Mark 2:2, groups "gather" naturally. In Matthew 25:35-43, the verb takes on a moral hue: welcoming the hungry, the stranger, the sick, is to "gather" them in charity. The image is that of the meeting, whether voluntary or summoned, of separated elements.
G4863.portee: This word invites the reader to reflect on the importance of the assembly: the Christian community exists only when gathered, united as one body around Christ. It also reminds us that welcoming others — the stranger, the poor, the sick — is a form of communal gathering: it is to integrate them, to receive them into communion. For the disciple, "to gather" is both to participate in church life and to open one's heart to those in need.

sens: Assembly of Jews gathered for worship and religious instruction
Building where this assembly takes place
Action of gathering together
Collection, gathering of things
G4864.detail:
1. The synagogue is primarily an assembly: a group of Jews who meet regularly, especially on the Sabbath, to pray, read the Scriptures, and learn. Jesus regularly taught in these assemblies (Luke 4:16; Acts 18:4), and it was an important place in His mission in Galilee (Matthew 4:23).

2. The word also refers to the building where this assembly takes place. When it is said that Jesus "entered the synagogue" in Capernaum or Nazareth (Mark 1:21; Luke 4:16), it refers to the physical place, the worship space built to accommodate the Jewish community.

3. Originally, the Greek word simply means "gathering" or "action of bringing together." It comes from two roots: "syn" (with) and "agogé" (to lead, to guide), hence the idea of "leading together."

4. By extension, the word can refer to any collection or gathering of things — for example, a gathered harvest, or collected money — but in the New Testament, it almost always applies to the Jewish assembly or building.
G4864.origine: The Greek word συναγωγή is composed of συν ("with") and ἀγωγή ("action of leading," from the root ἄγω, "to lead"). The initial image is therefore that of "leading together," of "gathering." In classical Greek, the word could refer to any gathering, but in the Bible, it primarily translates the Hebrew עֵדָה (edah, "assembly, congregation") and קָהָל (qahal, "assembly, multitude"), terms that denote the people of Israel gathered. The word has retained this specifically religious meaning in the New Testament.
G4864.emploi: The word appears 57 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the four Gospels and in Acts. It is a dominant feature of Jesus' ministry: He teaches in the synagogues of various towns in Galilee (Matthew 4:23, 9:35; Mark 1:39), particularly on the Sabbath (Mark 1:21; Luke 4:16). Acts shows Paul continuing this practice: he preaches in the synagogues of every city he visits (Acts 9:20; 13:5, 14; 18:4), making it the natural point of contact between the gospel and the Jews of the diaspora. The context also reveals the social structure of the synagogue — it had "chief seats" (Luke 11:43; Mark 12:39), leaders — and it could be a place of persecution against the disciples (Matthew 10:17; Acts 22:19). The word also occasionally applies to a Christian assembly (James 2:2).
G4864.portee: Understanding the word "synagogue" helps to see how Jesus and His disciples integrated into the Jewish life of their time. Rather than immediately breaking away from Jewish institutions, Jesus used the synagogue as a platform to teach and heal. Similarly, Paul always began in the synagogue to proclaim the Gospel to the Jews. This shows the New Testament's respect for existing religious structures and the desire to evangelize first from the heart of the Jewish faith. The synagogue also represents the contrast between two ways of living faith: some Pharisees sought honor there (Luke 11:43), while Jesus came to teach and serve.

sens: To struggle together, share a common effort
To support someone in their fight through prayer or action
G4865.detail:
1. The verb describes a struggle carried out by several, where each brings their strength to the same fight. The image is that of warriors or athletes fighting side by side, or helping a friend in their struggle. In Romans 15:30, Paul asks the Christians in Rome to "fight with him" — not with weapons in hand, but through prayer addressed to God on his behalf.
2. More broadly, "to fight with" means to support, to back someone in their effort or pain. It is to share not only the visible effort but also the spiritual stakes hidden behind it. When Paul invites the Romans to fight with him through their prayers, he is bringing them into his apostolic struggle as allies in the same fight.
G4865.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "sun" (with, together) and the verb "agonizomai" (to struggle, to fight). The latter comes from "agon," which primarily refers to sports competition or physical combat. The root evokes the image of an inner struggle or a pitched battle. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, the idea is close to "milhamah" (war, combat), but "to fight with" adds the Greek emphasis on shared effort and solidarity.
G4865.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 15:30. Paul, at the end of his letter to the Romans, urgently asks the assembly to "fight with him" by offering prayers to God on his behalf. The context shows that Paul is facing resistance, perhaps within the Christian community itself, and he invites them to support him through intercession. It is a call to fervent and supportive intercession, grounded in the love of the Spirit.
G4865.portee: This word reminds us that prayer is not a passive or solitary activity, but an active participation in the spiritual battle of those we love. To pray for someone is truly to "fight with them" — it is to become their invisible ally before God. For today's reader, it is an invitation to take intercession seriously: praying for pastors, missionaries, the persecuted, is to enter into the same spiritual struggle alongside them.

sens: To fight side by side, together, for a common cause
To strive jointly to defend or promote something
To participate in a fight, in a literal or figurative sense, alongside others
G4866.detail:
1. The word expresses the idea of fighting or struggling, but always in the company of others: it is a shared fight, a common struggle. When Paul writes to the Philippians (1:27), he speaks of "fighting together" for the Gospel — a warrior image to describe the collective determination of Christians in the face of obstacles.
2. It is also to strive together, in the sense of active solidarity. In Philippians 4:3, Paul asks his faithful companion to help those women who have "fought" alongside him for the Gospel: they have worked, toiled, and struggled together with him against obstacles and hostility.
3. The verb emphasizes less violence than shared commitment and collective perseverance: it is walking together toward a common goal, supported by others and supporting them in turn.
G4866.origine: The word is composed of "syn" (with, together) and the verb "athléô" (to fight, to struggle, like an athlete in the arena). The initial image is that of a sports or warrior fight, but made collective by the prefix "syn." It is a word from the family of "athlete" and "agon" (struggle, fight). Paul uses it to qualify the Christian life as a common participation in the same fight: all believers are in the same arena.
G4866.emploi: This verb appears twice in the New Testament, and both occurrences are found in Paul’s letter to the Philippians. In 1:27, he exhorts the church to stand firm "fighting together" for the faith of the Gospel, with one soul. In 4:3, he speaks of women (Euodia and Syntyche, likely) who have "fought" alongside him for the progress of the Gospel. These two uses show that Paul sees the Christian life, and particularly the defense of the Gospel, as a fight where unity and solidarity matter as much as individual courage. The context of Philippians is one of persecution or opposition: to fight together is to resist together.
G4866.portee: This word reminds Christians that they are never alone in their faith. The fight for the Gospel — whether preaching, witnessing, or living according to God's word in a hostile world — is a collective adventure. Paul values those who fight alongside him, both women and men: it is an invitation to see other believers not as spectators, but as comrades in arms. Solidarity is not a luxury; it is a form of courage.

sens: Bring a group of people together in one place
Gather together, group together
G4867.detail:
1. Gather means to call or bring people together so that they are in the same place. It is the action of one who calls others to come together, like Demetrius who gathers the craftsmen to inform them of the danger posed by Paul's preaching (Acts 19:25). The image is that of a convocation, an intentional grouping.
2. It also refers to coming together, grouping oneself — the action of several people coming together. During Peter's imprisonment, many Christians had gathered at Mary's house to pray together (Acts 12:12). The word evokes an organic regrouping, a convergence.
G4867.origine: The word is formed from two elements: "sun" (with, together) and "athroizô" (to assemble, to gather). The root "athros" literally means "assembled in a crowd" and connotes the idea of noise and tumult that accompanies a gathering of people. The word thus comes from the image of a noisy crowd coming together. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this verb generally translates "qabats," which also means to gather, collect, unite.
G4867.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Acts (12:12 and 19:25). In both cases, it describes a concrete gathering of people. In Acts 19:25, it is an active action: Demetrius gathers the workers to mobilize them. In Acts 12:12, the verb in the passive indicates that people had gathered at Mary's house. The context of these uses shows that the word concerns urgent gatherings related to important circumstances: persecution and mobilization against the Gospel.
G4867.portee: This word reminds us of the power of communion. In both biblical cases, people gather: the disciples to pray in crisis, or adversaries to conspire. It shows that gathering can serve faith as much as it can oppose it. For the Christian, it is an invitation to value gathering with other believers, this convocation that brings strength and comfort.

sens: Account for what one owes or has received
Ask someone to explain how they used what was entrusted to them
Demand payment of a debt or justification of one's management
G4868.detail:
1. This verb depicts the action of "making accounts": a creditor or master gathers what is due, lays the figures side by side, to see who owes what. In Matthew 18:23, a king wants to "give an account" — that is, settle his accounts — with his servants who manage his money.
2. The word also evokes the act of demanding an account, the interrogation of the servant who must explain his management: "When he began to settle accounts, one was brought to him who owed ten thousand talents" (Matthew 18:24). It is the moment of administrative judgment.
3. Finally, it designates the requirement itself: "he made them give an account" (Matthew 25:19), which imposes on the servant to justify his work and finances before his master. It is a weighty responsibility: one must prove that they have managed well what has been given to them.
G4868.origine: The word combines the prefix "syn" (together) and the verb "airô" (to lift, to carry). The starting image is that of "lifting together," then "assembling to make the account." This Greek word often translates in the Greek Old Testament the Hebrew verb "azab" (to leave, to forsake), but in the New Testament, Matthew uses it in its administrative sense: to settle a matter in common, to establish accounts.
G4868.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament, only in Matthew, always in connection with judgment and responsibility. It appears in two parables: that of the king who wants to give an account to his servants (Matthew 18:23-24) and that of the master who demands accounts from his stewards (Matthew 25:19). In both cases, it is about definitively settling accounts, confronting the one who has received a charge with what they must answer for. The context is always serious: there is a debt, a shortcoming, a correction to come.
G4868.portee: These two parables teach that every believer will give an account to God for how they have used what has been entrusted to them: talents, money, time, responsibilities. The phrase "give an account" reminds us that the management of our resources is not without consequence and that a day will come for judgment. This invites faithful and conscious management of what God has given us, and mercy towards those who owe us something, as the first servant should have shown towards his fellow servant.

sens: One who shares the condition of being a prisoner, especially a prisoner of war
