In a figurative sense, one who suffers with another for their faith in Christ
G4869.detail:
1. The word properly designates someone who is captive or imprisoned at the same time as another person. It is the sharing of a common captivity, a common deprivation of freedom. In Romans 16:7, Paul greets Andronicus and Junias as his "fellow prisoners," which evokes a bond forged in shared suffering.
2. In Paul's epistles, the meaning extends to those who suffer with him for the Gospel, even if captivity is not always physical at the time he writes. Aristarchus is called a "fellow prisoner" in Colossians 4:10, and Epaphras in Philemon 1:23: these men have endured or are enduring the same trials as Paul for their attachment to Christ. It is a spiritual solidarity sealed by suffering.
G4869.origine: The Greek word is composed of two elements: "syn" (with) and "aichmalos" (captive of war). It literally means "one who is captive with" someone. The basic image is military: captives taken together during a battle. Paul transposes this image to describe those who share with him the trial of imprisonment or persecution for the Gospel.
G4869.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in Paul's epistles. In Romans 16:7, Andronicus and Junias are presented as Paul's fellow prisoners and are held in high regard among the apostles. In Colossians 4:10, Aristarchus bears this title, confirming that he has shared the apostle's chains. In Philemon 1:23, Epaphras is called this "in Christ Jesus," which shows that this captivity is not a misfortune suffered passively, but a testimony of faithfulness to Christ. The context suggests that Paul honors these companions in trial by naming them thus.
G4869.portee: This word reminds the reader that suffering for Christ creates a deep bond among believers. Being a fellow prisoner of Paul means having paid a price for one's faith, and it is a title of honor, not shame. It shows that Paul views these trials not as defeats, but as marks of apostolic authenticity and devotion to the Lord.

sens: Go with someone, follow in their footsteps
Be present alongside someone in an important moment
Remain faithful to someone by following them
G4870.detail:
1. The most direct meaning is to go together with a person, to walk or advance at their side. In Mark 5:37, Jesus only allows Peter, James, and John to accompany him to Jairus' house, meaning to come with him into that house.
2. The word also emphasizes being present with someone, particularly in decisive or difficult moments. In Luke 23:49, the women who had accompanied Jesus from Galilee stand near the cross: they remain by his side to support him in his death.
3. It can express a form of loyalty or attachment to follow someone in their movements or path. The young man in Mark 14:51 followed Jesus to stay with him, even during the dramatic pause at Gethsemane.
G4870.origine: The word is composed of the prefix σύν ("with") and the verb ἀκολουθέω ("to follow"). This root evokes the image of walking behind someone, following in their footsteps. The addition of the prefix "with" reinforces the idea of a shared and supportive presence, not just a distant pursuit.
G4870.emploi: This verb appears three times in the Gospels, always to describe the act of walking or being alongside Jesus. Mark and Luke use it to show the disciples and the women who faithfully remain with Jesus: Peter, James, and John who follow him, the young man at Gethsemane, the women at the foot of the cross. The word emphasizes a personal and voluntary presence, often in a context where being with Jesus costs something or requires courage.
G4870.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader that following Jesus is literally walking with him: being his companions, remaining by his side in ordinary moments as well as in trials. It invites a concrete and visible loyalty, not just a simple heart adherence. The women at the foot of the cross embody this accompaniment to the end.

sens: Gather together, be assembled with others
Share a meal, eat together
Be in the company of someone
G4871.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of gathering, being assembled with other people in the same place. It conveys the idea of forming a group, being together. In Acts 1:4, Jesus "was found" with his disciples: he was gathered with them, present among them.
2. The word can also evoke the idea of sharing a meal together, eating in company: "finding" someone can mean "being at the table with" them, which creates a special communion.
3. More broadly, it means being in the company of someone, being close to them, maintaining their presence beside them. The word emphasizes proximity, a relationship of sharing the same space and time.
G4871.origine: The verb is composed of two elements: "syn-" (together, with) and a root meaning "salt" or "halium" (related to the Greek "hals"), which suggests the ancient image of a table community gathered around salt. This composition primarily evokes the communion created by sharing a meal, before taking on the broader meaning of simple gathering or assembly.
G4871.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 1:4, where Luke uses the present participle to describe Jesus being gathered with his disciples after his resurrection. This unique usage shows Jesus at the heart of his apostles, sharing their company and giving them his final instructions before the Ascension. The context suggests a particular intimacy: Jesus "was found" with them, remaining to teach them.
G4871.portee: This word reminds us that the risen Jesus does not abandon his disciples: he remains with them, present to comfort and prepare them. For the believer, it is an assurance that Jesus Christ stays with his people and continues to be in the company of those who follow him.

sens: Climb a height together with someone
Accompany someone in an upward movement or to a high place
Join someone to go to a location
G4872.detail:
1. The word designates the physical action of climbing together: ascending a slope, a mountain, or reaching a higher place in the company of others. In Mark 15:41, it refers to women who "went up" with Jesus from Galilee to Jerusalem, a city situated on high ground.

2. More broadly, the verb expresses the idea of accompanying someone on a journey or movement, particularly to an important or prestigious place. In Acts 13:31, those who "went up" with Jesus from Galilee to Jerusalem became his witnesses: this is not just a physical journey, but a relationship of companionship and loyalty.

3. The meaning can also include the idea of joining a movement, following someone in an endeavor or cause. These disciples who go up with Jesus demonstrate their attachment and commitment to him.
G4872.origine: The verb is composed of three elements: "syn" (with), "ana" (upward), and "baino" (to go, to walk). It literally expresses the action of going upward together. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, this kind of expression is conveyed by the verb "to go up" or "to ascend" (עָלָה, ʿalah), often used for pilgrimages to Jerusalem. The Greek composition "syn-ana-baino" is particularly expressive in describing collective accompaniment in an upward movement.
G4872.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the Greek New Testament, and both occurrences are in the Gospels and Acts. In Mark 15:41, Jesus ascends to Jerusalem accompanied by women who served him in Galilee; in Acts 13:31, after the resurrection, those who went up with Jesus from Galilee to Jerusalem become his official witnesses to the people. In both cases, the verb emphasizes both the physical journey to the holy city and the lasting relationship between Jesus and his companions: it is not a simple trip, but the expression of a community of life and testimony.
G4872.portee: This verb reminds us that following Jesus is not a solitary and abstract adherence, but a shared path with other believers. The women in Mark 15:41 and the apostles in Acts 13:31 demonstrate concrete loyalty: they rise, they depart, they go up with him. For the Christian reader, this word speaks to the importance of community in faith and the visible commitment that accompanies discipleship: one does not follow Jesus alone, one goes up with others toward the city of God.

G4873.fr: to be at the table with
sens: To share a meal reclining next to someone
To be seated as a guest at a banquet or feast
To participate in a meal of honor or celebration
G4873.detail:
1. The primary meaning is very material: to be lying down or sitting next to someone during a meal. In Matthew 9:10, tax collectors and sinners come "to the table" with Jesus and his disciples: they take their place with him to eat together. It is the simple act of sharing food in a resting position, as was done in the Greco-Roman world by reclining on couches around a low table.
2. The word also designates the quality of being a guest in a solemn or prestigious context. When Mark 6:22 speaks of Herod's "guests" watching his daughter's dance, it refers to the honored guests of a royal banquet. Similarly, in Luke 14:10, those who are "at the table" with you are the other guests of the feast: being with them means sharing their status as guests.
3. By extension, it means participating in a moment of communion or intimacy. In Luke 7:49, "those who were at the table" with Jesus observe his act of forgiveness: being at the table with him means witnessing his actions, entering into a shared moment that binds the guests together.
G4873.origine: The Greek word συνανάκειμαι is formed from three elements: συν ("with"), ανά ("together"), and κειμαι ("to lie down, to be seated, to rest"). The basic image is that of a body lying at the table, a habit of the ancient Mediterranean world. The root κειμαι evokes a position of rest, hence the notions of peace and intimacy associated with the shared meal. The prefix σύν at the beginning makes the action collective and relational.
G4873.emploi: The verb appears 7 times in the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, always in meal scenes. It designates either the action of taking a place at the table with Jesus (Matthew 9:10, Mark 2:15), or the position of a guest at a banquet (Mark 6:22 with Herod, Luke 14:10, Luke 14:15). The word emphasizes the closeness and relationship created by the sharing of a meal: in Luke 7:49, Jesus' guests form a united group that reacts together to his words. The context varies from a simple meal to a royal banquet, but the word always highlights the bond created by the common table.
G4873.portee: In the Bible, eating together is never neutral: it is an act of covenant and mutual acceptance. When Jesus is "at the table" with tax collectors and sinners, he affirms that he welcomes them, that they are his guests, his companions. For the reader, this word reminds us that the Eucharist extends this radical act of hospitality: being at the table with Jesus means entering into communion with him and with his brothers. It is a word of inclusion and grace.

sens: The act of mixing, mingling together
Frequenting, regular contact with someone
The act of communicating, exchanging with someone
Communion or association for a common purpose
G4874.detail:
1. The word carries the concrete image of mixing: when two things mix together, they blend. In 1 Corinthians 5:9, Paul uses this word to describe what should not be done: not to have "relationships" with the immoral, meaning not to mingle with their lives, not to associate with them.
2. Beyond physical mixing, the word signifies regular acquaintance with a person: it is maintaining habitual contact, sharing time together. In 1 Corinthians 5:11, Paul applies it to someone who claims to be a brother but lives poorly: one should not even eat with him, a gesture that symbolizes communion and fellowship.
3. The word can also refer to direct communication: the exchange of words or gestures between two people. In 2 Thessalonians 3:14, Paul says not to have "communication" with one who does not obey his letter.
4. Finally, the word can evoke a deeper association, a communion of life or common interests; but in the three Pauline uses, it is always in the negative: it is about breaking such communion.
G4874.origine: The Greek word is composed of three elements: the prefix "syn" (together), the prefix "ana" (again, in return), and the root "mignumi" (to mix). This composition suggests the idea of mutually mixing, mingling with one another bilaterally. The base verb "mignumi" (to mix) originally expresses the physical action of blending two things. Here, applied to people, it means sharing someone's life, allowing oneself to be influenced by their company.
G4874.emploi: Paul uses this verb three times, all in the context of church discipline. In 1 Corinthians 5:9 and 5:11, he commands the Corinthians not to have "relationships" with believers who live in sin (immorality, greed, idolatry, drunkenness, extortion, etc.). This is not a call to monastic withdrawal, but to separation from those who bear the name of Christian while refusing to live according to the Gospel. In 2 Thessalonians 3:14, Paul uses the synonym "communication" to denote the opposite act: one must keep away from the one who does not obey the apostolic instructions, so that he may feel ashamed and return. The Pauline context is always pastoral: it is about correcting, bringing back to obedience, not condemning definitively.
G4874.portee: This word reminds Christians that separation from evil is sometimes a duty of love. Refusing "relationships" with one who lives in sin is not malice, but a call to repentance. At the same time, the Pauline precision (one must eat with the non-Christian, 1 Corinthians 5:10) shows that this separation is not an absolute rupture, but a way of saying: your life matters, your choices have consequences. It is an exhortation to community vigilance and the collective holiness of the Church.

sens: To rest together, to sleep together
To be spiritually refreshed in the company of others
G4875.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: to rest or sleep side by side with someone. It is the image of shared relaxation, the calm found in the presence of others.
2. The Bible uses this word in a spiritual sense: to be comforted, revitalized in spirit in the company of brothers and sisters. In Romans 15:32, Paul says he hopes to "enjoy some rest among you" — not just physical rest, but a peace of heart and spiritual consolation received through fellowship.
G4875.origine: The word is composed of three Greek elements: σύν (syn, "with"), ἀνα (ana, "again"), and παύω (pauo, "to cease", "to stop"). The idea is one of a common cessation, a shared rest. This composition evokes mutual rest, not solitary. In Isaiah 11:6 (in the Greek translation of the Old Testament), the same word translates a Hebrew verb meaning "to lie down, to rest."
G4875.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 15:32. Paul uses it to express his desire to meet the church in Rome and to find, in their company, not only the rest of the journey but especially the comfort and spiritual edification that fellowship provides. It is a mutual rest, where each one strengthens the other by their presence.
G4875.portee: This word reminds the reader that the Christian is not made to live alone: true rest and peace are also found in brotherhood. When we gather with other believers, it is not just a simple break; it is an opportunity to mutually strengthen one another in faith. Paul desires this kind of rest with the Romans, showing that even the apostles needed fellowship and fraternal support.

sens: Come to meet someone, go to meet them
Find oneself face to face with someone
Welcome someone by going to meet them
Arrive, occur (of an event)
G4876.detail:
1. The primary meaning is literal: to go to meet someone, to head towards them to join them. This implies intentional action, often involving movement: Peter enters somewhere and Cornelius goes to meet him to receive him (Acts 10:25), or Melchizedek goes to meet Abraham who is returning from battle (Hebrews 7:1).
2. More simply, the verb means to meet someone, to be in the presence of someone after having sought or awaited them: the disciple must meet a man carrying a pitcher in the city (Luke 22:10).
3. The expression "to go out to meet" is an idiom: it expresses respectful or honorific welcoming, eagerness to receive someone important (Hebrews 7:10). It is a gesture of deference or honor.
4. Figuratively, the verb can mean to arrive or occur, as when an event "meets" us, that is, comes to us, reaches us: Paul does not know what will happen to him in Jerusalem (Acts 20:22).
G4876.origine: The Greek word συναντάω is composed of σύν ("with") and ἀντάω ("meet, face"), suggesting the image of two paths crossing, of two people finding themselves together in the same place. In Hebrew, it translates several verbs: פָּגַע (pāga') and פָּגַשׁ (pāgash), which also mean to meet or go to meet, and קָרָא (qārā') or קָרָה (qārah), which mean to happen or occur.
G4876.emploi: The verb appears 6 times in the New Testament, mostly in Luke and in the Epistle to the Hebrews. Three uses describe a literal meeting with the sense of going to meet: a crowd comes to meet Jesus (Luke 9:37), Cornelius goes to meet Peter (Acts 10:25), Melchizedek went out to meet Abraham (Hebrews 7:1, 7:10). One use designates a future meeting: the disciple will meet a man in Jerusalem (Luke 22:10). Only one usage is figurative, to signify an event that occurs: what will happen to Paul (Acts 20:22). The context determines whether the word emphasizes the action of going to meet, the simple fact of meeting, or an event that happens.
G4876.portee: This verb reminds us that encounters with others — especially with Jesus — are not accidents. To go to meet someone is also to deliberately place oneself in their presence, with respect or affection. For the Christian, it emphasizes how God places the people and situations we need in our paths, and how responding with eagerness and honor is a proper attitude.

sens: Take part in an effort, in a burden
Support someone by sharing their load
Intervene to rescue or assist
G4878.detail:
1. The word paints the image of someone standing beside a person to help them carry something. Martha asks Jesus to tell Mary to help her with the household tasks (Luke 10:40): she has work to do, and she needs someone to share this burden with her.
2. It also means to support someone in their weakness or difficulty. The Spirit helps us in our weakness when we pray (Romans 8:26): He does not abandon us in the face of our limits, He stands by our side to support us.
3. More broadly, the word means to intervene with someone to help them, to provide concrete or spiritual assistance.
G4878.origine: The word is composed of three parts: "syn" (with), "anti" (facing, beside) and "lambanô" (to take). The basic image is that of someone standing beside another person to take or carry something with them. It conveys the idea of joint help, of sharing the burden. The same image appears in the Greek Old Testament when speaking of helping to carry something or supporting someone.
G4878.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the New Testament (Luke and Romans). It is always used to describe concrete or spiritual help provided to someone in need. In Luke, Martha seeks material help to accomplish her tasks. In Paul, the Holy Spirit helps us spiritually in our prayer, interceding for us when we do not know how to pray. The word emphasizes that help involves an active and supportive presence, not mere permission or tolerance.
G4878.portee: This word reminds Christians that true help, whether fraternal or divine, is standing beside someone to share their burden. It does not consist of ignoring the difficulty of others, but of actively intervening. And the most precious: the Holy Spirit Himself helps us in our spiritual weaknesses, interceding for us. It is a word of comfort and assurance.

sens: Be carried away, led by a force or influence that pushes us against our will
Allow oneself to be dominated by an opinion or practice that one joins through conformity or weakness
Adapt, conform to the way of life of others
G4879.detail: 1. The word evokes the image of a person being carried away by a current or pulled by an irresistible force. In Galatians 2:13, even Barnabas, a companion of Paul, was "led away" by the hypocrisy of the Jews returning to their old practices: he did not resist, he allowed himself to be carried along by the movement. 2. It is less about physical violence than moral seduction: one is led towards a bad attitude or problematic behavior, often without truly wanting to, by group pressure or a lack of firmness. In 2 Peter 3:17, the reader is warned not to be "led away" by the error of depraved men, that is, not to let themselves be contaminated by their false doctrines. 3. The verb can also designate voluntary accommodation to the conduct of others: in Romans 12:16, it refers to agreeing with those who are humble, conforming to their spirit rather than remaining stiff in one's pride.
G4879.origine: The Greek word is composed of συν (with) and απάγω (to lead away, carry off). This composition suggests the idea of sharing a common direction, of being led together or in the same direction as others. The basic image is that of movement: something pulls us along with it.
G4879.emploi: The verb appears only three times in the provided New Testament. In Galatians 2:13, Paul reproaches Barnabas for being led away by Jewish hypocrisy in Antioch. In 2 Peter 3:17, the apostle warns believers not to be led away by the error of unprincipled people. In Romans 12:16, Paul exhorts to accommodate to humble feelings, not to be led away towards pride. The context is always moral or spiritual: it concerns an influence that can lead us astray from righteousness.
G4879.portee: This word reminds believers of their vulnerability to group pressures and the seduction of conformity. It invites vigilance: even the strongest in faith risk being led away if they let their guard down. It also calls for cultivating a peaceful resistance and a solid personal conviction, rather than mechanical obedience to others.

sens: Die at the same time as another person
Share in someone's death, be united with them in death
Choose to suffer or make the ultimate sacrifice alongside someone
In a spiritual sense, be associated with the death of Christ through faith
G4880.detail:
1. The literal meaning is to die at the same time as another person. Peter asserts that he is ready to die at the same time as Jesus rather than deny him (Mark 14:31).
2. More broadly, it means to share in someone's death, to be bound to them in what is the most extreme trial. Paul speaks of living and dying with the Corinthians, referring to the deep bond their faith creates (2 Corinthians 7:3).
3. To accept making the ultimate sacrifice, to suffer with the one you follow. This is the meaning of Peter's commitment: he is ready to go all the way, even to death.
4. In 2 Timothy 2:11, the word takes on its richest spiritual dimension: being dead with Christ means that the believer has participated in his death through faith in baptism and conversion, uniting their old life to the Savior's cross.
G4880.origine: The word is composed of three elements: συν (sun = with), ἀπό (apo = away from, separation) and θνήσκω (thnēskō = to die). The basic image is that of dying together, sharing the same fate. The preposition "with" (sun) indicates association, communion in action. It is a word created to express a shared death or participation in the death of another.
G4880.emploi: The word appears only three times in Greek in the New Testament, always in a context of personal commitment or spiritual communion. Mark reports Peter's promise: he proclaims that he is ready to die with Jesus. In 2 Corinthians 7:3, Paul speaks of the pastor's solidarity with his people in life and death. But the most theological use is found in 2 Timothy 2:11: "If we died with him, we will also live with him" — this is the heart of Paul's doctrine of the believer's union with Christ. Dying with him is not literal, but a spiritual reality: it is the death of the old man and the entrance into a new life.
G4880.portee: This word reveals the depth of what it means to follow Jesus: it is not a superficial adherence, but a real communion in his death and resurrection. For the believer, "dying with Christ" is not a threat, but the hidden promise that this death leads to eternal life with him. It is through this mysterious participation in his death that we find our true life.

sens: be destroyed or annihilated together with someone else
be engulfed in the same ruin as another
share the same fate of death
G4881.detail:
1. This verb expresses the idea of disappearing, being annihilated together with others — not in isolation, but sharing the same destructive fate. It is a solidarity in destruction, a common ruin. In Hebrews 11:31, Rahab "did not perish with the rebels": she should have been engulfed in the destruction of Jericho that struck them all, but her faith saved her from that collective fate.
2. The word emphasizes the communion of fate: those who perish together are bound by the same threat, the same judgment that reaches them. This is why Rahab, although living in a condemned city, escapes the common death that the unbelievers around her will experience.
G4881.origine: The verb is composed of three Greek elements: "syn" (with), "apo" (away, separation) and "ollumi" (to destroy, to lose). This construction emphasizes that it is not just a simple destruction, but a destruction that binds the one who perishes to others in the same fate. The preposition "syn" meaning "with" marks the idea of community, of solidarity in misfortune. The word often translates the Hebrew idea of being engulfed together (from the verb "saphah").
G4881.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 11:31. It describes the context of the fall of Jericho: while the city and its rebellious inhabitants are destroyed, Rahab the prostitute, who had welcomed the Israelite spies, escapes this collective destruction. Her act of faith and kindness isolates her from the judgment that strikes others. This passage uses the verb in the passive voice to show that she did not share the fate of the unbelievers, contrary to what could have happened.
G4881.portee: This word reminds us that faith can preserve us from the judgment that reaches those who reject God. Rahab, although living among a rebellious community, was saved by her trust in God and her welcoming of those who served him. It invites us to reflect on our own faithfulness to God in a world that turns away from him, and on the power of faith to spare us from collective judgment.

sens: Send someone in the company of another
Have someone accompanied by a messenger or an envoy
G4882.detail:
1. The verb συναποστέλλω combines three ideas: "with" (συν-), "away from" (απο-), and "send" (στέλλω). It designates the action of sending someone while having them accompanied by another person. It is to send two people together, one going to the recipient while the other escorts or assists them.
2. In 2 Corinthians 12:18, Paul says "I urged Titus to go to you, and with him I sent the brother": this means that Titus does not go alone, but that a brother accompanies him, sent in the same movement to be with him. It is a coordinated sending where both messengers go together to fulfill the same mission.
G4882.origine: The word comes from three Greek elements combined: συν (with) + απο (away, at a distance) + στέλλω (to place, to send). The simple verb στέλλω means to prepare and send someone; the addition of "with" and "away" creates the idea of an accompanied sending. It is a word from administrative and religious correspondence: when one entrusts a mission to someone, one can send them alone or send them with a companion.
G4882.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 12:18. Paul uses it to clarify that when he asked Titus to go to the Corinthians, he did so while sending him with a brother. The apostle then poses a rhetorical question: since Titus and the brother were sent together and walked "in the same footsteps", neither of them demanded or committed injustice. The verb emphasizes the unity of action and loyalty between the two envoys.
G4882.portee: This word reminds us that the messengers of the Gospel are never alone: they can be sent with others for a common mission, to help each other, to witness together, and to ensure their integrity through mutual presence. It is an image of brotherly communion in the service of God.

sens: Assemble pieces so that they fit perfectly
Assemble the parts of a whole so that it functions as a harmonious unit
Arrange the elements of a structure with harmony and solidity
G4883.detail:
1. The verb primarily evokes technical adjustment: assembling stones, beams, or parts of a construction so that each fits well with the others, without gaps or cracks. This is the idea of the carpenter or mason who builds a structure (Ephesians 2:21).

2. Then, it applies to the living parts of a body: the members, the organs coordinate so that the whole is alive and effective. Each part fulfills its function, guided by the head, and everything adjusts for the growth and harmony of the whole (Ephesians 4:16).

3. In a broader sense, it conveys the idea of a structure that holds firmly because all its elements are well articulated. It is not just about placing them next to each other, but binding them so that they form a coherent and functional whole.
G4883.origine: The word is composed of two Greek elements: "sun" (together, with) and "armologeô" (to adapt, adjust). At its root, we find "harmos" (joint, articulation) and "legô" (to put together, assemble). The image is that of the joint, the natural connection between two bones that allows them to move in harmony. In ancient Hebrew, this idea of harmonious assembly is expressed by words evoking solidity and cohesion.
G4883.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the letter to the Ephesians. In Ephesians 2:21, Paul uses it to describe the spiritual building of the Church under construction: believers from all nations are assembled as living stones that fit together, forming a holy temple. In Ephesians 4:16, he applies the same image to the body of Christ: the members, coordinated by ligaments and guided by the head, grow together. These two uses show that "coordinate" refers to the divine action that unites believers not by mechanical juxtaposition, but by a living and functional bond.
G4883.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to understand that the Church is not a mere collection of individual believers, but a living organism where each person has their place and role. Just as a body only lives if its members are well adjusted and work together, the Church fulfills its mission only if each member of Christ exercises their gift in harmony with others, all under the direction of the head, who is Jesus. This calls for communion, mutual aid, and shared responsibility.

sens: Take someone or something forcefully and carry it away
Keep someone firmly in one's power
Be carried away, drawn by an irresistible force
G4884.detail:
1. Seize and carry away: the word describes a brutal and sudden action — one grabs something or someone and forcefully drags them elsewhere. In Acts 19:29, the crowd "drags" Gaius and Aristarchus to the theater, taking them against their will. It is a violent and determined movement.
2. Hold under control: the word can also mean to keep someone captive, to hold them seized. In Luke 8:29, the demon "had seized" this man for a long time and "kept" him — he held him in his power, chained and tortured, without letting go.
3. Being carried away by a power: when one undergoes the action, the verb expresses being swept away without the ability to resist. In Acts 27:15, the ship is "driven" by the wind — it can no longer fight and must let itself drift, dominated by the storm.
G4884.origine: The word combines the prefix "with" (syn-) and the verb "to seize" (harpazō). This root harpazō evokes a brutal, almost violent taking — like grabbing a spoil or snatching something away. The prefix reinforces the idea: to seize together, to carry away in one go. In the Greek Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew verb "to take" (laqach), expressing a resolute and firm action.
G4884.emploi: The verb appears four times in the Greek New Testament, always in contexts of applied force. In Luke 8:29, it describes the enduring control of a demon over a person — an ancient and tyrannical grip. In Acts 6:12 and 19:29, it reports how someone is forcefully seized to be taken somewhere: Stephen is arrested by the Sanhedrin, Paul's companions are dragged to the theater by the furious crowd. In Acts 27:15, the meaning changes: it is not a person who seizes, but a natural force that drives the ship despite all efforts. The word always emphasizes a power that masters and dominates.
G4884.portee: This verb reminds the reader of two major realities: first, the reality of spiritual warfare — a demon can seize a person and hold them captive, as in Luke 8:29; secondly, persecution — those who follow Jesus can be seized and carried away by human hostility, like the apostles. But it also invites us to ask: what are we seized by? Are we carried away by powers contrary to God, or firmly held by Christ?

sens: To push and develop in the same place and at the same rate
To mix in a common growth, without possible distinction until the end
G4885.detail:
1. The word describes a natural process of parallel growth: two plants growing side by side, in the same place, nourished by the same soil and water. This is the case of wheat and tares in the parable of Matthew 13:30: they grow together in the same field, and it is impossible to uproot them separately without damaging the wheat.

2. The meaning extends to any situation where two realities develop together without being able to be separated: they grow in such intimacy that they cannot be distinguished until they reach maturity. The parable teaches that the children of the kingdom and those of the evil one will grow side by side until the final judgment, where only God can separate them.
G4885.origine: The word is composed of two elements: "syn-" (together) and "auxanō" (to grow, to increase). It is a natural formation in Greek to express the idea of common growth. The simple verb "auxanō" often appears in the New Testament to speak of the growth of the kingdom of God or the Church.
G4885.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 13:30, in the parable that Jesus explains to his disciples. It designates the parallel growth of the wheat and the tares in the same field. It is a technical and vivid word, chosen by Matthew to emphasize the impossibility of separating these two realities until they are mature. The context is intentionally agricultural, as Jesus speaks to listeners who are well acquainted with harvesting.
G4885.portee: This parable reassures the Christian: the presence of evil alongside good in the Church and the world is not a problem to be solved immediately by our efforts. Jesus affirms that the final judgment will be the work of God alone, who will perfectly distinguish what we cannot discern. This invites patience and humility in our attempts at communal purity.

sens: That which physically connects two things together
That which unites the members of a body into a coherent whole
That which binds a person to a negative or destructive reality
That which unites believers together in a shared spiritual life
G4886.detail:
1. In the literal sense, a link is an object that attaches, ties, or holds together — like a rope or a ligament. The Bible uses this word to speak of the joints and ligaments that maintain the human body in its unity (Colossians 2:19).

2. Figuratively, the link refers to what binds the elements of a group or a whole. It is the image of the body: believers are "assisted and firmly joined together by joints and links" (Colossians 2:19), illustrating how the Church holds together.

3. The word can name what chains, what paralyzes: Simon the Sorcerer finds himself "in the bonds of iniquity" (Acts 8:23), meaning trapped by sin like by invisible chains.

4. Finally, the link is what unites believers in their common life. "Charity" is the "bond of perfection" (Colossians 3:14), and the "bond of peace" preserves "the unity of the Spirit" (Ephesians 4:3): that which attaches us to one another in faith.
G4886.origine: The Greek word σύνδεσμος comes from συν ("together") and δέω ("to bind"). Its starting image is therefore literally "that which binds together." This compound formation reflects its biblical usage well: it always designates something that unites, ties, or creates cohesion among several elements, whether physical or spiritual.
G4886.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, only in the Pauline epistles. In Colossians 2:19, it describes the natural ligaments of the human body. In Acts 8:23, Colossians 3:14, and Ephesians 4:3, Paul uses it figuratively to speak of what binds believers: sometimes what chains them to evil (Acts 8:23), sometimes what unites them in good — peace, charity, perfection. The word always illustrates a deep reality: something that creates an inseparable union, for better or for worse.
G4886.portee: This word reminds Christians that they are never isolated: they are linked to other believers by invisible but real bonds. It is a call to take the unity of the Church seriously, not as a mere theory, but as something as concrete as a ligament in a body. It also invites us to examine which "link" we obey: the one that chains us to sin, or the one that unites us to Christ and His people.

sens: One who is chained, locked up against their will
Figuratively: being bound, held by a force or obligation
Being united with someone in the same condition of captivity or suffering
G4887.detail:
1. The word concretely describes a person who is chained or locked up, deprived of freedom — one who bears chains or is held prisoner. This is the basic image of the word, which comes from the verb "to bind together."

2. Figuratively, the word can also refer to one who is bound or held by an invisible force: a habit, a passion, a guilt, or an obligation that chains the soul as chains confine the body.

3. Especially, in Hebrews 13:3, the apostle exhorts Christians to "remember the prisoners," meaning to think of those who suffer imprisonment with compassion, as if they themselves were enduring that suffering, for all believers form one body. The word invites empathy and solidarity with the persecuted.
G4887.origine: The Greek word συνδέω is born from two elements: σύν ("with, together") and δέω ("to bind"). The image is that of chains that bind together, that attach. It translates the Hebrew שָׁבַץ and other verbs of captivity. The prefix "together" reminds us that the prisoner is bound, held as one ties things together.
G4887.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in Hebrews 13:3. The apostle uses it in the passive voice — "you who are prisoners"... not literally, but in spirit, as he calls free Christians to feel united with those who suffer imprisonment for the faith. It is a call to memory and compassion for the martyrs and the persecuted, based on the unity of the body of Christ.
G4887.portee: This word teaches us that the sufferings of persecuted brothers should not be foreign to us. Even if we are not in prison, we are called to carry them in our hearts as if we were with them, for we form one body in Christ. It is a challenge to true sympathy and prayer for those who pay the price for their faith.

sens: To share in someone’s glory, to be honored together with them
G4888.detail: 1. The verb literally means "to be glorified together." It describes the action of participating in the glory, honor, and dignity of someone else. In Romans 8:17, Paul explains that Christians who suffer with Christ will also be glorified with Him: sharing in His sufferings, they will also share in His final glory in the Kingdom of God.
G4888.origine: The word is composed of "sun" (together, with) and "doxazô" (to glorify, honor, give glory). The root "doxa" (glory) evokes splendor, honor, recognized dignity. This rare composition in Greek of the New Testament emphasizes the idea of shared participation: one is not only glorified, but glorified together with another, which implies a union and a shared destiny.
G4888.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Romans 8:17, in the passive voice (to be glorified). Paul uses it to comfort Christians who endure persecution and suffering: if you suffer with Christ, you will also be glorified with Him. It is a promise of shared fate — present suffering and future glory shared together.
G4888.portee: This word reminds Christians that present suffering is inseparable from future glory: we are never alone in our trials, but linked to Christ Himself. It also affirms that our glory will not be individual and solitary, but common with Jesus, which infinitely enriches the promise. For the believer facing the difficulties of faith, it is a radical perspective of hope and identification with the risen Christ.

sens: servant who works with another under the same master
one who shares the condition of servant or slave
brother or sister in Christ sharing the same divine service
G4889.detail:
1. In a concrete sense, the companion in service is a servant who works alongside another servant under the authority of the same master. In the parable of Matthew 18:28, it is literally another slave who owes money to the first servant.

2. More broadly, it refers to one who shares the same condition of dependence or subordination. Epaphras in Colossians 1:7 is called a "companion in service" because he serves Christ, just like Paul and his readers.

3. In a spiritual sense, the word designates a brother or sister in Christ who shares the same commitment to service toward the Lord. In Revelation 6:11, the martyrs are seen as companions in service, all submitted to the same divine Master, all engaged in the same cause.
G4889.origine: The word is composed of σύν (syn, "with") and δοῦλος (doulos, "servant"). It literally designates one who is a servant with someone else. The root δοῦλος evokes the condition of slave or subordinate servant, a strong image in the New Testament to express the relationship between the believer and God.
G4889.emploi: The word appears ten times in the New Testament. Matthew uses it three times (18:28, 18:29, 18:31, 18:33, 24:49) in contexts of human servants working together. Paul uses it twice (Colossians 1:7 and 4:7) to describe Epaphras and Onesimus as his collaborators in the service of Christ. Revelation uses it four times (6:11, 19:10, 22:9) to designate heavenly servants — martyrs, angels — who share the same divine service. The word always emphasizes a relationship of equality in subordination to the same authority.
G4889.portee: This word reminds Christians that they are never alone in their service. Whether engaged in an ordinary task or in witnessing their faith, they share this responsibility with other believers placed under the same authority of Christ. It is an invitation to solidarity, to compassion towards those who walk with us (as the contrast in Matthew 18:28-33 illustrates), and to recognize our common dignity as servants of the same Master.

sens: a gathering of people rushing en masse to the same place
a throng of agitated people, often tumultuous
G4890.detail: 1. The word describes an influx of crowd: many people pressing and hurrying together towards the same point. It is the image of the mass converging. In Acts 21:30, when Paul is accused in the temple of Jerusalem, "the whole city was stirred up, and the people rushed together from all directions": it is this sudden influx of crowd that rushes in. 2. By extension, it is a gathering characterized by agitation and disorder, often of a hostile or tumultuous nature. The context of Acts 21 illustrates this nuance well: it is not just a simple gathering, but an agitated crowd that rushes upon Paul to mistreat him.
G4890.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "syntrechō" which means "to run together, to press together." It is formed from "syn" (together) and "trechō" (to run). The image is that of mass movement, of people running in the same direction. This term often translates in Greek the realities of an agitated crowd or a disorderly gathering. It is a specifically Greek word to describe this urban phenomenon of sudden convergence of people.
G4890.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 21:30. It describes the critical moment when Paul, arrested in the temple of Jerusalem, is seized by a frenzied crowd that drags him outside. The usage is concentrated: it serves to show the violence and immediacy of the people's reaction, the sudden influx of an agitated mass. It is a term chosen to express not a peaceful gathering, but a convergence of crowd characterized by emotion and agitation.
G4890.portee: This word reminds us how the Bible describes moments of crisis where reason gives way to collective emotion. The crowd here acts as one body, without discernment or justice — it is a lesson on the power of mass movements and the fragility of the circumstances surrounding the service of God. For the believer, it illustrates the dangers of being swept away by collective emotion and the importance of remaining anchored in truth rather than blindly following what the crowd does.

sens: to lift up together, to make rise in concert
In a spiritual sense: to be raised at the same time as Christ
To share in the resurrection of Christ in the believer's experience
G4891.detail:
1. In the literal sense of the word, it is the action of raising or making several people rise together — the image is that of people being lifted off the ground at the same time. But the Bible does not use this word for an ordinary physical action.

2. The spiritual sense completely dominates: "to be raised with Christ" means that the believer is associated with the resurrection of Jesus. It is not just a future promise: it is a present reality for the Christian, a change that is applied to him right now. In Colossians 2:12, we see this spiritual resurrection linked to baptism and faith: the believer who has been baptized and who believes has already been raised to a new life with Christ.

3. This shared resurrection transforms the believer's life here and now. In Ephesians 2:6, Paul affirms that we are already "seated in heavenly places" with Christ — this means that our life is united to the glorious life of the risen Jesus. In Colossians 3:1, the consequence is clear: if you have been raised with Christ, then seek what is above, where he is seated.
G4891.origine: The Greek word is composed of "sun" (with) and "egeirō" (to raise, to awaken, to resurrect). This combination creates the idea of "to raise together." It conveys Paul's movement of including the believer in the event of Christ's resurrection: not simply waiting for a future resurrection, but recognizing that one already participates spiritually. It is a powerful image of the bond between Christ and the Christian.
G4891.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, always in Paul's writings and always in the passive voice ("we have been raised," "you have been raised"). This indicates that it is God who raises the believer, never the believer who raises himself. The three occurrences are found in two related epistles: Ephesians and Colossians. In Ephesians 2:6, it is an accomplished act: God "has raised us up." In Colossians 2:12, the spiritual resurrection is inseparable from baptism and faith. In Colossians 3:1, it becomes the foundation of a moral exhortation: "seek the things above." The word thus expresses both a stated truth and a life to be lived.
G4891.portee: This word reveals the Christian conviction that the resurrection of Christ is not a distant and past event, but that it concerns us already now. The believer does not live waiting to "become" resurrected one day: he is already so in Jesus. This assurance transforms prayer and daily life: since we are raised with Christ, we can already seek "what is above" instead of being attached to earthly concerns. It is a source of freedom and new priorities.

sens: Assembly or local tribunal of the Jews
The supreme court and official judicial assembly of the Jewish people
G4892.detail:
1. The word primarily designates any assembly or local tribunal that judges and renders justice. It is a council of judges. Jesus teaches that whoever is angry with his brother is liable to be brought before such a tribunal (Matthew 5:22), and the apostles are warned that they will be delivered to these local assemblies (Mark 13:9).

2. It mainly refers to the Sanhedrin proper, the supreme court of the Jews in Jerusalem, composed of the elders, chief priests, and scribes. It is this body that judges Jesus himself during his trial (Luke 22:66, Matthew 26:59), and that convenes to judge the apostles after Pentecost (Acts 5:21, Acts 22:30). The word can also refer to the meeting place of this assembly (Acts 4:15).
G4892.origine: The Greek word συνέδριον comes from σύν ("with") and ἕδρα ("seat"), hence the image of "sitting together." It is therefore a council or assembly where judges sit side by side to deliberate. The Hebrew and Aramaic word סַנְהֵדְרִין (sanhedrin), of which it became the Greek equivalent, has the same origin: הדרים סנ, "those who sit together." This institution has its roots in the judicial organization of Israel, although it took its historically known form especially during the Second Temple period.
G4892.emploi: The term appears 22 times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in the Gospels and Acts. It primarily designates local tribunals, assemblies of judges in synagogues or cities of Judea (Matthew 10:17, Mark 13:9). But its major usage concerns the Sanhedrin of Jerusalem, the supreme court. Matthew and Mark mention it during the trial of Jesus (Matthew 26:59, Mark 14:55, Mark 15:1). Luke emphasizes the solemn assembly of those who judge him (Luke 22:66). Acts constantly refers to it: the Sanhedrin meets to interrogate the apostles (Acts 5:21), Paul appears before it (Acts 22:30, Acts 23:1, Acts 23:6), and we see the internal tensions that divide it between Sadducees and Pharisees (Acts 23:6). The word also applies to the meeting place (Acts 4:15). Its role in the New Testament is therefore to remind of the Jewish religious and judicial authority before which the apostles testify about Jesus.
G4892.portee: The Sanhedrin represents in the New Testament the established religious authority of Israel, the one that condemned Jesus and persecuted the early Christians. Its history in Acts shows that the testimony of the disciples is expressed not in silence, but in the face of authority, and that they joyfully accept to be judged and to suffer rather than to deny (Acts 5:41). This invites the reader to see that true moral authority belongs to the one who obeys God rather than to humans (Acts 5:29), and that religious persecution should not deter from testimony.

sens: Inner knowledge, immediate feeling of what is happening within oneself
Innate moral discernment that judges our actions, thoughts, and words
Inner voice that accuses or approves depending on whether one acts rightly or wrongly
State of purity or guilt before God in the secret of the heart
G4893.detail:
1. The word primarily designates conscience as the knowledge one has of oneself, inner lucidity: it is the feeling of what is happening in our mind and heart. Hebrews 10:2 uses it in this way, speaking of those who would be "purified" in conscience, meaning they would feel innocent.

2. But above all, conscience is this moral discernment that God has engraved in every human being: an innate ability to recognize right from wrong, without needing to learn it. This is what Paul describes in Romans 2:15, where even non-Jews "without the law do naturally what the law requires," for their conscience commands them.

3. Conscience accuses: it denounces the wrong committed. It is what "accused" the accusers of the adulterous woman, silencing them (John 8:9). It torments one who has acted wrongly, even if he is not seen. It can also approve: having a "good conscience" or a "pure conscience" (1 Timothy 1:5, 2 Timothy 1:3) means feeling in one's heart that what one does pleases God.

4. Conscience can become corrupted or desensitized. A "weak" conscience (1 Corinthians 8:7, 8:10) does not dare assert its freedom because it is chained by doubt; a "bad" conscience (Hebrews 10:22) weighs on us like a permanent condemnation. That is why Paul emphasizes the importance of maintaining a "pure" or "blameless" conscience—a state of inner peace where one does not judge oneself.
G4893.origine: The Greek word συνείδησις (suneidēsis) comes from συν (sun = "with") and εἴδησις (eidēsis = "knowledge"). It literally means "knowledge-with-self," in other words, the awareness one has of one's own actions. It is a late Greek word, absent from Homer, but it becomes common in Stoic thought and among post-classical authors. It enters Christian language through the New Testament itself. In Ecclesiastes 10:20, it is also found to translate the Hebrew word מַדָּע (madda, "knowledge").
G4893.emploi: This word appears 30 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Pauline epistles, but also in Peter and in the epistle to the Hebrews. Paul uses it primarily in Romans and 1 Corinthians to speak of moral conscience: the one that reproaches us for wrongdoing (Romans 9:1, where Paul affirms "with great sorrow of heart" that his conscience bears witness), or the one that must be protected by not forcing those who are weak to violate their convictions (1 Corinthians 8:7, 8:10, 8:12). In 1 Corinthians 10:25-29, it concerns practical conscience regarding idols: should one eat meat sacrificed to idols? Paul says that conscience itself matters less than love for one's neighbor. In Hebrews 9:14 and 10:22, conscience becomes what must be purified by the blood of Christ, moving from a bad conscience to a conscience at ease before God. In Peter (1 Peter 2:19, 3:16, 3:21), conscience is what supports the believer who suffers unjustly.
G4893.portee: Conscience is, according to the Bible, the inner witness that God has placed in every human. That is why it cannot be extinguished without violence: it is proof that God speaks to all men, even to those who do not know the written Law. For the believer, maintaining a "pure" or "good" conscience is not a matter of feeling or weakness—it is a sign that one walks in truth and submits to Christ. It is only in Him, through His sacrifice, that one can be freed from a bad conscience and live with the peace of one who knows he is forgiven.

sens: To be aware of something, to be conscious of it
To understand together, to grasp at a glance
To reflect, to weigh a situation mentally
G4894.detail:
1. To be aware of something or to be conscious of it: this means to see with one's mind what is happening. In Acts 5:2, Sapphira knew (she was aware) that her husband was keeping back part of the price of the sold property. It is a clear and personal knowledge of the facts.

2. To understand together, to grasp in a single mental act: the word evokes the idea of seeing an entire situation at a single glance of the mind. It is to weigh, examine, reflect in order to fully grasp what is happening.

3. To reflect, to weigh a situation in order to make a decision: in Acts 12:12, Peter, after having reflected (having fully grasped the situation), went to the house of Mary to seek help. It is the act of mentally concentrating to understand and act.
G4894.origine: The word is formed from "sun" (together, with) and "eidō" (to see). The starting image is therefore that of seeing together or seeing at a single glance. In classical Greek, it literally meant "to see at the same time." The meaning has enriched to also denote awareness, inner knowledge, and then mental reflection. It is a compound verb that emphasizes the overall or simultaneous aspect of knowledge.
G4894.emploi: The verb appears three times in Acts (5:2, 12:12, 14:6), always in contexts of moral awareness or thoughtful decision-making. In Acts 5:2, it denotes Sapphira's awareness of her husband's dishonesty. In Acts 12:12, it expresses Peter's act of reflection as he, aware of his situation, makes a decision. In Acts 14:6, the context suggests an awareness or understanding of the imminent threat. The word always emphasizes an inner, conscious, and clear knowledge, often related to decision-making or moral responsibility.
G4894.portee: This word speaks of our ability to know the truth — not just by hearsay, but through personal and clear awareness. It reminds us that we are responsible for what we know: Sapphira knew she was participating in a lie. In the believer's heart, the knowledge of God and His will is also an awareness that engages our responsibility. The Holy Spirit often acts by illuminating our conscience, giving us this clear view of the truth.

sens: to be present with someone
to accompany someone in an action or moment
to share someone's company
G4895.detail: 1. The verb simply describes the act of being present with a person, standing by their side. In Luke 9:18, Jesus is praying "alone," which implies that His disciples are not with Him — the verb here expresses absence or physical presence. 2. It can mean to accompany someone in what they are doing or experiencing. In Acts 22:11, Paul recounts that after his vision on the road to Damascus, the men who accompanied him "were with him" — they shared the experience of the journey and the extraordinary events. 3. More broadly, the word evokes the idea of companionship, of communion: being together in the same place or situation.
G4895.origine: The word is composed of σύν ("with") and εἰμί ("to be"), which literally gives "to be-with." It is a natural Greek construction to express simple coexistence or mutual presence. In Hebrew, the Old Testament often expresses this idea with the verb רעה or equivalent terms meaning "to be a companion of" or "to pasture together."
G4895.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament. In Luke 9:18, it appears in a textual variant where Jesus is alone to pray, raising the question of who is or is not with Him. In Acts 22:11, Paul speaks of the men who were with him at the time of his conversion, emphasizing their physical presence as witnesses to the event. The word remains simple and concrete: it does not describe a deep spiritual communion, but just the fact of being together, sharing a moment or a place.
G4895.portee: For the believer, this verb reminds us of the importance of presence — that of other disciples in critical moments, that of God Himself who "is with" His people. Although rare, it emphasizes that even in decisive spiritual experiences (Jesus' solitary prayer, Paul's conversion), the context of accompaniment and human testimony has its value.

sens: To gather in one place
To come together as a group
To converge to a common place
G4896.detail:
1. To gather in one place: the verb depicts the action of people coming together to the same location. In Luke 8:4, a great crowd assembles around Jesus, coming from various cities — this is the moment when people physically gather to listen to Him.

2. To come together as a group: it expresses not only the coming but the formation of a coherent group. The emphasis is on the result: isolated individuals become a united crowd, capable of hearing the same word together.

3. To converge to a common place: the verb suggests that several currents, several movements of people (here, from various cities) culminate at the same central point, thus creating an assembly.
G4896.origine: The word is composed of σύν (syn = "with, together") and ἔρχομαι (to come, to go). This composition is transparent: it literally means "to come together." The root ἰ/ἔρχ- (to go, to come) is a very common root in Greek for movements. The prefix σύν- adds the idea of communion or gathering.
G4896.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 8:4. Luke uses it to describe the moment when a great crowd gathers around Jesus, coming from several cities at once. It is a term that emphasizes the action of gathering rather than the crowd itself — we see the movement of people converging towards Jesus to listen to Him teach.
G4896.portee: This verb shows us how the word of Jesus creates attraction: people from different places move and gather. It illustrates the power of His teaching and the urgency that people feel to come and listen to Him. For the reader, it is a reminder that the Gospel gathers: it creates communion, uniting believers around the same word.

sens: to enter together into a place
to accompany someone by crossing an entrance
G4897.detail:
1. The verb designates the action of entering together into a place: two or more people cross a door or threshold at the same time or as a group. In John 18:15, this other disciple "enters" with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest, meaning he follows Him through the same passage.
2. By extension, the word emphasizes the idea of accompaniment and closeness: to enter with someone means not to stay outside, but to follow them or stay by their side while crossing a threshold. It is a gesture of solidarity or deference.
G4897.origine: The Greek word is composed of three elements: syn ("with"), eis ("into"), and erchomai ("to go, to come"). The basic image is that of walking together: several people move to enter somewhere. The family of the verb includes other movement words like "to depart," "to enter," "to exit." The root is simple and concrete: it represents a gesture that everyone understands.
G4897.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Gospel of John (6:22 and 18:15), always in the past tense to describe a specific event. In John 18:15, it is the action of this other disciple who follows Jesus to the high priest: he enters the courtyard at the same time as Him, which allows him to be present during the interrogations. The context shows that this act of entry has narrative importance: it is because he enters with Jesus that he can later observe the events and testify about them.
G4897.portee: This verb speaks to us of the discreet yet faithful presence of the disciples with Jesus, even in difficult or perilous moments. To enter with Him means refusing to abandon Him, even when danger threatens. It is a lesson on the cost of discipleship: following Jesus means joining Him wherever He goes, including to places where we might be afraid to go alone.

sens: one who travels with someone else
one who shares a mission or a common work
G4898.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to someone who physically travels with another person. In Acts 19:29, Gaius and Aristarchus are Paul's travel companions: they accompany him on his missionary journeys through the cities of the Mediterranean.
2. The meaning extends to one who shares a mission or spiritual work. In 2 Corinthians 8:19, Paul speaks of a travel companion chosen by the Churches to accompany him in his collection for the poor in Jerusalem: this is someone who participates in the same charitable work and bears the same testimony.
G4898.origine: The word is composed of two elements: "sun" (with) and "ekdēmos" (who is outside, absent from his homeland, traveler). It literally designates one who is "outside with" someone, that is, the companion in the journey or absence. This term emphasizes the shared nature of the experience: one does not travel alone, but together.
G4898.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in Paul's epistles. In Acts 19:29, it describes Paul's travel companions during his ministry in Asia Minor. In 2 Corinthians 8:19, Paul uses it to refer to a delegate from the Churches who accompanies him in his charitable collection mission. In both cases, the word underscores the idea of shared presence and collaboration: these men are not merely isolated travelers, but partners in a common endeavor, whether missionary or charitable.
G4898.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that serving God is not a solitary work. Paul surrounds himself with travel companions, both for practical and spiritual reasons: to share the work, support one another, and testify together to their commitment to the Church. It is an invitation not to undertake alone what God calls to do, but to seek brothers and sisters with whom to walk.

sens: one who has been chosen at the same time as others
one who shares in divine election
G4899.detail:
1. The word designates someone chosen together with others — as if selecting a group of candidates for a mission or dignity. The image is one of sorting, of selection. In 1 Peter 5:13, "the Church of the elect in Babylon" evokes all the believers in that place who have been chosen by God together as His people.
2. In a spiritual and biblical sense, it is to receive divine election — the status of those whom God has set apart for Himself. Peter greets not an isolated individual, but an entire community of the elect: those who, along with other believers in the world, have been chosen to belong to the people of God and participate in His salvation.
G4899.origine: The word is composed of three Greek elements: sun- ("with"), ek ("out of"), and lektos ("chosen," from legein, "to choose"). The basic image is that of choice, of sorting — separating something from the rest. When "with" is added, it conveys the idea of choosing together, sharing the same status of choice. The word "chosen" in French comes from the Latin electus, which translates this same Greek root.
G4899.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 5:13. Peter concludes his letter by referring to the greeting of "the Church of the elect in Babylon" — probably Rome, referred to here by a symbolic name. This unique occurrence shows how the adjective "elect" is applied to an entire Christian community: Peter speaks not of isolated individuals, but of the Church as the body of the elect, those whom God has chosen together to be His people.
G4899.portee: This word reminds the reader that becoming a Christian is not an isolated personal decision, but being integrated into a community of the elect — the Church. The use of the plural "elect" emphasizes solidarity in faith: believers are not alone in their divine choice; they are part of a people united by God's election. This strengthens collective identity and faithfulness.
